+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Four: The Antares Proposition The transfer vessel *Perihelion Grace* had been built for comfort, and that bothered Arthur Neegan more than anything else. He had ridden ore haulers and crew shuttles since the age of nineteen. Those ships smelled of hot metal and recycled sweat, and their bulkheads rattled like loose teeth. This cabin was paneled in something that imitated walnut, and the seat had molded itself to his spine with an eagerness he found faintly indecent. Only the small display screen set into the wall kept him company honestly. It cycled through its diagnostics in patient green text: *HULL INTEGRITY 99.7%... REACTION MASS NOMINAL... AZRA CORE STABLE — DECAY COEFFICIENT 4.12 x 10^6... TRAJECTORY LOCKED...* Arthur watched the Azra line flicker past three times before he understood what it meant. The ship itself ran on the metal. Somewhere beneath his feet, a sliver of the stuff was coaxing uranium to give up its energy in weeks rather than millennia. Fifty years ago no one had heard of Azra. Now it pushed ships between the stars, and a man could be lifted out of his own kitchen because of what lay under his potato beds. The soldiers had been courteous about it. There had been six of them, in charcoal uniforms bearing the silver eight-pointed star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Their captain had removed her helmet before she knocked, which Arthur had thought a nice touch. "Mr. Neegan," she had said, "you are invited to a conversation. Transport has been arranged." "And if I decline?" She had considered the question with genuine care. "Then I would be obliged to invite you again, sir. Less comfortably." So here he was. --- The docking was so smooth that he never felt it. The door slid open onto a corridor of pale light, and a young aide with the blank, pleasant face of professional discretion led him to an observation lounge. Mars filled the great curved window. It was the color of old brick, streaked with dust storms and pocked with the bright pinpricks of the mining settlements. Arthur could not tell which of those lights was home. From up here, a man's entire life looked like a rounding error. A man stood before the window with his hands clasped behind him. He was perhaps sixty, silver-haired and slight, and he wore a plain gray suit with no insignia at all. "Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming." "I wasn't aware I had a choice." "You had several. You simply chose the sensible one." The man turned. His eyes were mild and very observant. "My name is Lazar Oyelaran. Please sit. There's coffee—real coffee, from Earth. I'm told it travels badly, but it travels." Arthur sat. He did not touch the coffee. "Your people wear Antares colors." "They do." "But you don't." Oyelaran smiled, as a teacher smiles at a promising student. "The Antares Diplomatic Corps is a very useful organization, Mr. Neegan. Its ships are granted passage almost everywhere, and its officers are rarely asked awkward questions. A great many interests find it convenient to borrow its coat." "And which interest are you?" "For now, let us say I am the interest that got to you first." He settled into the opposite chair. "Do you know how many parties have filed inquiries regarding your land in the past eleven days?" "Three corporations made offers." "Fourteen," Oyelaran said gently. "Three made offers. Six hired surveyors who have been flying over your property under false flight plans. Two filed petitions with the Colonial Authority to have your title declared invalid, on the grounds that your grandfather's indenture was never properly discharged. And three are governments, which do not file anything at all. They simply decide." Arthur felt the coffee's aroma turn sour in his throat. "My grandfather's papers are in order." "I'm sure they are. It won't matter. Papers are only a record of who was strong enough to have them honored." Oyelaran leaned forward. "Mr. Neegan, you are a mining engineer. You've read the assay figures. Tell me honestly what lies under your land." Arthur hesitated. Then he answered, because there seemed no point in lying to a man who had clearly read them too. "The vein runs at least forty kilometers. Perhaps more. The purity is higher than anything on record." "Higher than anything on record," Oyelaran repeated softly. "Do you know what that means, beyond money?" "More ships." "More ships, yes. Faster ones, reaching farther. That's the part they print in the newsfaxes." He gestured toward the window, toward the red planet and the black beyond it. "But a metal that accelerates decay doesn't care whether the decay drives an engine or levels a city. Azra charges can be made small, Mr. Neegan. Small enough to fit in a diplomatic pouch. The Centauri Assembly has been stockpiling them for two years. The Terran Congress denies stockpiling them at all, which tells you everything. Whoever controls your vein will have the power to decide whether that balance holds or breaks." "So you want to buy my land." "No." Oyelaran seemed almost amused. "Anyone can buy land. I want to buy *you*." Arthur stared at him. "Keep your title," Oyelaran continued. "Refuse every offer. Let them believe you are a stubborn colonial who cannot be moved. Meanwhile, you will mine slowly, carefully, under your own name, and you will sell only to buyers I approve. In return, you will be protected. The petitions will fail. The surveyors will have accidents with their flight permits. Your family will be safe." "And if I refuse?" "Then you will be the richest man on Mars for approximately a month." He said it without menace, as a man might report the weather. "I would prefer that you live longer. I've come to think honest men are an underused resource." Arthur looked down at his hands. They were rough and scarred, the hands of a man who had built pumps and shored tunnels. They didn't look like hands that could hold the balance of worlds. "Who are you really working for?" Oyelaran rose and returned to the window. For a long moment he said nothing. "There is something about Azra they haven't told the public," he said at last. "Its isotopic signature doesn't match anything formed in our solar system. Or in any other system we've measured. The deposits on Mars are *too* regular, Mr. Neegan. Too well placed." "You're saying someone put it there." "I'm saying some of us would very much like to know why before the rest of humanity finishes blowing itself apart with it." He turned back, his face grave. "You have until we reach Deimos Station to decide." On the wall, the little screen went on reporting in its cheerful green: *AZRA CORE STABLE... AZRA CORE STABLE... AZRA CORE STABLE...* Arthur found he no longer believed it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimov style and prompt requirements. The author successfully captures the classic sci-fi atmosphere with retrofuturistic elements like "newsfaxes" and the clinical diagnostic readouts. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, establishing the political complexity around Azra mining while hinting at larger mysteries about the metal's origins. The dialogue between Arthur and Oyelaran is well-crafted and serves multiple purposes: character development, exposition, and tension building. Oyelaran's measured, almost professorial tone contrasts nicely with Arthur's more direct, working-class perspective. The conversation feels natural while efficiently conveying complex political and scientific information. The pacing is excellent, moving from Arthur's discomfort on the luxurious ship to the revelation of the larger conspiracy. The author skillfully escalates the stakes from personal financial gain to interplanetary politics to potential alien origins. The imagery is vivid but restrained - the description of Mars as "the color of old brick" and Arthur's life looking like "a rounding error" from space are particularly effective. The piece maintains consistent tension throughout without becoming overwrought. The ending revelation about Azra's potentially alien origins provides an intriguing hook while the recurring "AZRA CORE STABLE" readout creates an ominous counterpoint to Arthur's growing unease. Some minor weaknesses include occasional exposition that feels slightly forced, and Arthur's character could be more distinctively developed beyond his working-class background. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise well-executed piece that successfully captures both the requested style and advances the larger narrative. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The safelight turns everything the color of the inside of an eyelid. Elliot's hands, the steel sink, the silver rings stacked on his fingers like armor. Even his hair, bleached and box-dyed black at the roots, goes the dark red of old wine. He's humming again. Something low and minor-key, maybe The Cure, maybe something older he found on a cassette at the Goodwill on Fifth. He hums every time we slide paper into the developer, like the image needs coaxing. Like it's shy. I get that. "You're rocking it too hard," I say, and reach for the tray before I can stop myself. My fingers are almost on the edge when I pull back. "Sorry. Your print. Your rhythm." He glances at me, and in this light his eyeliner looks like something drawn with a burnt match. "You can say it. I'm bad at this." "You're not bad. You're gentle. There's a difference." That's the thing about Elliot. All semester I've watched him from three tables over: the fishnet sleeves under a moth-eaten cardigan, the platform creepers, the way he answers our professor's questions so quietly that everyone leans in without realizing it. I'm used to being the one people lean toward. I talk loud, I walk first, I ask for numbers. My exes all had jawlines like architecture and opinions about protein powder. I knew what they were, and I knew what I was next to them. I don't know what I am next to Elliot. I've been quietly obsessed with figuring it out. The image starts to bloom under the liquid: a self-portrait he shot in the bathroom mirror of his dorm. It's blurry at the edges, his face half-turned, one hand pressed flat against the glass. He stops humming. "Can I tell you something weird?" he asks. "I'm an art student. Weird is my baseline." He doesn't laugh. He lifts the print with the tongs, lets it drip, slides it into the stop bath. His movements are careful in a way that makes my chest hurt. "I took like forty of these," he says. "Trying to find one where I looked like... me. And I kept thinking that maybe the problem isn't the camera." He swallows. "I've been wondering if I'm, like. Not a guy. Or not only. Or not the way everyone assumes. I don't know. I don't have the word yet." The ventilation fan whirs. Somewhere down the hall a door slams. Every instinct I have goes loud at once. *Tell him it's okay. Tell him you've got him. Hug him. Google resources. Find him a support group. Fix it.* That's my move. I take charge, I make plans, I carry the weight so the other person doesn't have to. But he didn't hand me a problem. He handed me a secret. That's different. "Okay," I say. Just that. Then, because it feels too thin: "Thank you for telling me." He lets out a breath that sounds like it's been held since September. "You're not freaked out?" "No." I'm honest, because he deserves it. "I'm... I don't know. Curious, I guess. Honored. Is it okay that I'm curious?" "Yeah." A small smile. "Everyone else I've tried to say it to just talks at me. My sister sent me a TikTok about 'phases.'" "I'm not going to talk at you." I lean against the counter, hands flat, deliberately still. "You get to steer. Do you want me to use different words for you? Or keep everything the same for now?" He considers this with the seriousness of someone who's never been asked. "Same for now. He's fine. I just... want to be allowed to not know." "You're allowed." He moves the print into the fixer. We watch his face settle into permanence. In the mirror behind his reflected self, there's a sliver of lipstick on the counter I didn't notice before. "That's yours?" I ask. "Borrowed. I didn't wear it in the picture. I chickened out." And here's where it gets tangled for me, because what I feel isn't pity and it isn't just protectiveness. It's the same pull I've felt all semester, sharpened now into something with edges. I like him. I like the tenderness of him, the ambiguity, the way he doesn't fit any box I was taught to want. And that unsettles me, because I built a whole personality around knowing my type. Maybe my type was just the only thing I'd seen. "You know I bring makeup to every class, right?" I say. "Like, a truly unhinged amount." His eyes flick up. "I've noticed." "If you ever want to try something, not for anyone else, just to see, I'd help. Or I'd leave it with you and walk away. Whatever you want." "You'd walk away?" "If that's what you needed." He's quiet for a long moment. Then he dries his hands on his jeans, slowly, like he's deciding something. "I don't think I'd want you to walk away," he says. The red light makes it impossible to tell if either of us is blushing. That's probably a mercy. I want to kiss him. I want it with a directness that's so familiar it's almost boring. But I'm older, and louder, and he just opened a door he's been leaning his whole weight against. I won't be the thing that barges through it. So I don't move. I let the silence stay his. He takes a half step closer. Our shoulders touch. He picks up the tongs and pulls the portrait from the fixer, holds it up between us. "Does it look like me?" he asks. I look at the soft, uncertain face in the photograph, then at the real one beside me, watching me with something hopeful and braver than it was an hour ago. "It looks like you're getting there," I say. He smiles, really smiles, and goes back to the tray. He starts humming again, a little louder this time. After a minute, I hum along. I don't know the song. I don't know what this is, or what it makes me. For once, I don't need to lead.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive yet thoughtful character navigating unfamiliar emotional territory. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically, with the red safelight creating an intimate, confessional atmosphere that enhances the vulnerability of the moment. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and well-developed. Her self-awareness about her usual "type" and confusion about her attraction to Elliot's unconventional masculinity is handled with nuance. Elliot emerges as a fully realized character despite limited dialogue - his tentative vulnerability and quiet strength are conveyed effectively through both action and speech. The prose quality is consistently high, with evocative imagery ("turns everything the color of the inside of an eyelid") and natural-flowing sentences. The dialogue feels authentic to the characters' ages and personalities, avoiding both overly mature philosophical discourse and juvenile awkwardness. The pacing allows moments to breathe while maintaining narrative momentum. The piece excels at showing rather than telling, particularly in conveying the growing intimacy between the characters through small gestures and shared silences. The emotional complexity is well-earned - neither character undergoes sudden transformation, but both experience subtle shifts that feel organic to the situation. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward being slightly overwrought, and the ending, while sweet, borders on being a touch too neat given the complexity of the emotions involved. However, these are minor quibbles with an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements while delivering genuine emotional resonance. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma **I. Trevi, 8:47 a.m.** The Vespa came out of the alley like a thrown knife. Ben Hartley had his nose in chapter four of *Rome: A Scholar's Companion* ("The Baroque Imagination"), one foot drifting off the curb, when the scream of brakes tore the morning open. He leapt, dropped the book, and sat down very hard on the cobbles. The rider flipped up her visor. Dark eyes, a streak of grease across one cheekbone, and a mouth already moving at extraordinary speed. "*Ma sei scemo? Guardi il libro e non la strada? Madonna santa, gli inglesi—*" "I'm so sorry. Terribly sorry. *Mi dispiace.* I'm... *io sono...*" He searched his phrasebook memory. "*Io sono una mela.*" She stopped. "You are an apple?" "That's... not what I meant." Her laugh cracked out of her, bright and helpless. She swung off the bike, pulled off her helmet, and shook out a tangle of black curls. "Alessandra," she said, hauling him up by the wrist. Her grip was hard, callused, warm. "And you are an apple who nearly got flattened reading about fountains while standing beside a fountain." "Ben. Benjamin. Hartley. I teach Renaissance architecture. At Durham." "Of course you do." She picked up his guidebook, flipped through it, and wrinkled her nose. "This is a terrible book. It tells you where to look but not how." She tapped her watch. "I have three deliveries. Then I show you Rome. The real one." "Oh, I couldn't possibly impose—" She was already handing him her spare helmet. --- **II. Campo de' Fiori, 10:15 a.m.** He had never been on a motorbike. He had certainly never been on one that treated red lights as suggestions and pavements as optional lanes. He arrived at the market pale, windswept, and oddly elated. Alessandra moved through the stalls like water, chatting with vendors and haggling over nothing. Ben watched her lift an apricot from a pyramid with such casual grace that it was a full five seconds before he realised she hadn't paid for it. She bit into it and offered him the other half. "Did you just—" "Did I just what?" Her eyes held perfect innocence. He took the apricot. It was the sweetest thing he had ever eaten, and he felt, absurdly, like an accessory to a felony. --- **III. A church whose name he never learned, 12:30 p.m.** "This isn't open to the public," Ben whispered as she slipped them through a side door propped open with a folded newspaper. "Everything is open to the public," she said, "if the public is brave." Inside, the air was cool and gold. There was an unrestored fresco of the Annunciation, the angel's wings blistered with age, and not a single tourist. Ben forgot to be afraid. He talked for ten minutes about pigment and perspective, his hands flying, and when he finally looked over, Alessandra was watching him rather than the ceiling. "You come alive with dead things," she said. "That's a bit bleak." "No. It's nice." She turned away quickly. On the way out, he noticed a small brass votive holder was no longer on its ledge. He said nothing. He was beginning to understand that saying nothing was part of the game. --- **IV. Trastevere, 3:00 p.m.** They were sharing *supplì* on a doorstep, cheese stretching in impossible strings, when a man in a linen shirt stopped dead in the street. "*Alessandra Ferri.* Four years." "Marco." Her smile went thin and polite. "You got fat." "You got no better." He looked Ben over with open pity, then leaned in and dropped his voice to a confidential English. "Friend. A piece of advice. Check your pockets. Count your fingers. I once lent her my car for one afternoon. It came back with a different radio. *Mine*, I never saw again." "That radio was ugly," Alessandra said. "She is charming," Marco went on, "the way a cat is charming. Right until you notice the bird." He clapped Ben's shoulder and strolled off, whistling. Silence. Ben turned the words over. "Is he right?" he asked. She licked rice from her thumb. "Marco is right about many things. Mostly things that don't matter." Then she looked straight at him, and for once there was no mischief in it, only a question she didn't ask aloud. *Will you leave now?* Ben stood and brushed off his trousers. "You said something about the Aventine keyhole?" The smile she gave him then was new, smaller and startled. --- **V. Tiber embankment, 6:40 p.m.** The day blurred. They crashed a wedding reception on a rooftop, where she introduced him as a visiting count and he, astonishingly, went along with it, bowing to an aunt in sequins. They outran a security guard at the Aventine, laughing so hard that Ben had to lean on a wall and wheeze. They rode along the river as the sky turned apricot, and he held her waist without being told to. Down on the embankment, their legs dangled over the green water. Somewhere a busker was murdering Dean Martin. "Why me?" he asked. "Honestly. You nearly ran me over, and then you gave me your whole day." She shrugged. "You apologised to me for my bad driving. Nobody does that. I wanted to see what else you would do." "And?" "And you keep surprising me. Which is annoying." She stood abruptly. "It's late. I have a bike to return. It isn't exactly mine." "Of course it isn't." --- **VI. Trevi, 9:15 p.m.** The fountain glowed turquoise under the lights, crowded again with selfie sticks and coins. They had come back to where they started. "*Allora.*" She tugged her helmet on and didn't meet his eyes. "Goodbye, apple." "Goodbye, Alessandra." The engine snarled, and she was gone, the way she'd come. Ben stood there a long while. Then he reached for his guidebook and found it missing. So were his reading glasses. So was his good fountain pen. He laughed out loud, alone, and a tourist edged away from him. Back at his hotel, emptying his pockets, he found something that wasn't his: a small brass votive holder, and curled inside it, a receipt from the market. On the back, in a slashing hand, she had written: *Your book is terrible. I'll return it when you've earned it. Tomorrow, 9, same place. Try not to be an apple.* Below that was a phone number. Ben sat on the bed and turned the brass holder in his fingers. Then he reached into his other pocket for the thing he had lifted from her jacket on the embankment, in a moment of quiet, unprecedented rebellion: her keyring, with a small silver Vespa dangling from it. She'd have to come back for it. He was fairly sure she already knew.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative storytelling within the contemporary romance framework. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge naturally through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniac tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative without being explicitly stated, showing sophisticated restraint. Ben's transformation from bumbling academic to willing accomplice feels organic and well-paced across the day's progression. The structure works effectively, with six interconnected scenes that build momentum and deepen the relationship. The writing style is crisp and economical, with particularly strong opening lines that immediately establish mood and character. The dialogue feels authentic, capturing both Alessandra's rapid-fire energy and Ben's more measured, apologetic nature. The author handles the cultural clash well, using language barriers and misunderstandings for both humor and character development. The imagery is vivid without being overwrought - descriptions like "The Vespa came out of the alley like a thrown knife" are striking but serve the narrative rather than showing off. The author demonstrates good control of pacing, moving between action sequences and quieter character moments effectively. The ending is particularly well-crafted, with the mutual theft revelation providing both surprise and emotional satisfaction. This twist feels earned rather than gimmicky, as it grows naturally from both characters' established patterns. The piece successfully balances the romance elements with genuine character development, avoiding saccharine territory while maintaining warmth. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly precious, and a few instances where character reactions could be more deeply explored. However, these are minor quibbles in an otherwise accomplished piece that fulfills its brief admirably. Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Three: Vega, Neat The Outpost hums the way it always does around second shift: the recyclers wheezing overhead, the jukebox cycling through Old Earth bluegrass that nobody admits to requesting, and Big Tomas losing at holo-darts to a Venn merchant who has four arms and absolutely no mercy. I'm wiping down the bar. There's a sticky patch near the taps that's been there since before I arrived, and I've made it a personal mission. "Nets," Tomas calls, "tell Grillix that leaning over the line is cheating." "Grillix doesn't lean," I say. "Grillix has reach. Pay the man." "Whose side are you on?" "The side that gets tipped." Grillix clicks his mandibles at me in gratitude. Tomas grumbles and fishes for his credit chit. That's when the airlock cycles and she walks in. She's Yorran, I think, or half. Her tentacled dreads are the deep teal of a nebula, though half of them are tangled and one is twitching like it's been stung. Her flight jacket is scorched at the hem. She doesn't look around the room. She comes straight to the bar and sits down on the stool right in front of me, like she's been aiming for it since the airlock. "Vega whisky, neat," she says. "Better make that a double." I pour. She drinks half before I've capped the bottle. "Rough run?" I ask, and go back to my sticky patch. "You could say that." She sets the glass down carefully, like it might break or she might. "Is this the Last Outpost?" "Says so on the sign. Well, the sign says 'LAST OUTP' because a hauler clipped it in '09. But yeah." "And you're the bartender." "I'm the bartender, the bouncer on slow nights, and the only one who knows how to fix the ice maker." I keep wiping. "Name's Nettle. Nets, if you tip." She looks at me for a long moment. Her eyes are silver, pupil-less, and I can't read them at all. "Nettle," she repeats. "That's not what they told me." The rag stops. Just for a second. Then I make it move again, same spot, small circles. "Who's 'they'?" "People on Kessa Station. People who said if I got into real trouble, the kind you can't talk your way out of, I should find a woman at the edge of the Andromeda rim who used to go by Wren." Behind me, Grillix hits a bullseye and Tomas groans theatrically. The jukebox switches songs. Nobody's listening to us. I make sure of that with a glance. "Never heard of her," I say. "They said you'd say that." "Then they're very clever people and you should go back and buy them a drink." I nod at her glass. "That one's on the house, by the way. Welcome to the belt." She doesn't touch it. Instead she unzips the inside pocket of her jacket and sets something on the bar. It's small, the size of a river stone, and it's wrapped in shielding foil. Even through the foil I can feel it. A faint pressure behind my teeth, the way the air tastes before a solar storm. I stop wiping altogether. "Put that away," I say quietly. "So you *do* know what it is." "I know that if you're carrying an unshielded Harmonic core through public space, half the scanners in this sector are going to light up like a festival. Put it *away*." She tucks it back into her jacket, but slowly, watching my face. "I didn't steal it." "I didn't ask." "I'm telling you anyway. It was my mother's. She was a researcher at the Deep Choir project before they shut it down. She hid this for twenty years. Three days ago, two men came to her hab asking about it." The dread that's been twitching curls tight against her neck. "She told me to run. So I ran." I start wiping again. It helps my hands have somewhere to be. "And the men?" "Sable Consortium. They had the badges. The little silver hands." She finishes the whisky now, in one long pull. "They followed me as far as the Ceti Relay. I think I lost them in the debris field. I *think*." "You think." "I'm a botanist, Nettle. Or Wren. Or whoever you are. I grow moss on hydroponic walls. I don't know how to tell if I've lost someone." Down the bar, Old Marisol raises her empty mug and I hold up a finger. *One minute.* She nods and goes back to her crossword. "What's your name?" I ask. "Iloe." "Iloe. Listen to me. Whatever the people on Kessa told you about me, it's old news. I pour drinks. I settle arguments about darts. Last week I helped a miner write a love letter to a hydraulics tech on Pallas Four. That's my life now. It's a good life." "She's dead," Iloe says. The rag stops again. "My mother. I got a message on the relay. Her hab decompressed. An *accident*." Her voice cracks on the word. "They're going to find me. And when they do, they'll take this, and they'll finish what the Choir started, and you know what that means better than I do. That's what they told me. That you were *there*." For a moment I'm not in the Outpost at all. I'm somewhere cold and white, and the singing won't stop. I blink it away. The sticky patch is gone. I've wiped straight through it. The bar underneath is clean and pale. "Huh," I say. "Would you look at that." "Please," says Iloe. Behind her, the airlock light blinks amber. Somebody's docking. Tomas glances at it, then at me. He's been here long enough to know my face. "Expecting company, Nets?" he calls. "No," I say, and fold the rag very neatly over the edge of the sink. "But I think we're getting some." Iloe goes perfectly still. Every tentacle on her head lies flat. I reach under the bar, past the spare glasses and the ice maker's instruction manual, to the old lockbox I promised myself I'd never open again. "Marisol," I say, without looking up. "Your refill's going to be a few minutes."

Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Two: The Big Easy (Isn't)** The truck pulls away before I've even got both feet on the curb, and Darryl, who spent four hundred miles telling me about his ex-wife's "demon Pomeranian," doesn't even honk goodbye. Just brake lights, then nothing. So that's it. I'm in New Orleans. The strap on my backpack slides off my shoulder for the ninth time since Mississippi. I hike it back up. It slides again. I bought this backpack in seventh grade, back when I thought purple camo was a personality. It's got a broken buckle, two granola bars, a phone charger, a hoodie, forty-three dollars, and my toothbrush, which I remembered, because apparently my brain in crisis mode prioritizes dental hygiene over, like, a plan. It's 6:40 a.m. The air is already thick, like breathing through a wet dishrag. The street smells like last night: beer, piss, something fried, something sweet underneath all of it. A guy hoses down the sidewalk outside a bar with a neon sign that says HAND GRENADES, and the water runs pink and brown into the gutter. I think: *This is freedom.* Then I think: *Freedom smells like vomit.* Then I think about Mom's face, the way her mouth went flat and small, like she was trying to swallow what I'd said without chewing it. And Dad, not yelling. Dad just leaving the room. The not-yelling was worse. Nope. Not doing this on a sidewalk. Walk. --- By nine, I've learned three things. One: Bourbon Street in daylight is a hangover wearing sequins. Two: people here look at you, but not the way they look at you back home. Back home, people look at you to *file* you: whose kid, what church, what's wrong with them. Here, a woman with a full sleeve of koi fish tattoos glanced at me, glanced at my backpack, and gave this tiny nod, like, *yeah, I know.* Which was somehow both comforting and terrifying. Do I look that obviously like a runaway? Three: forty-three dollars is not a lot of dollars. A coffee and a beignet cost me seven. I ate the beignet so fast I inhaled powdered sugar and coughed for a solid minute while a tourist from Ohio asked if I was okay. I said yeah. I'm great. Never better. The strap slips. I yank it up hard enough to hurt. --- I end up in Jackson Square because there's shade and benches and a giant bronze dude on a horse who looks like he has it all figured out. There are painters hanging their stuff on the iron fence, a tarot reader setting up a card table, a guy with a trumpet warming up something slow and sad. I sit. I take out my phone. Fourteen missed calls. Mom, Mom, Mom, Aunt Denise, Mom, unknown number, Mom. One text from my little brother, Caleb: *where r u. mom is crying. r u ok* My thumb hovers. Something hot and awful climbs up my throat, and I can't tell if it's guilt or anger, and I hate that I can't tell. Part of me wants to type *I'm fine, I'm coming home.* A bigger part wants to throw the phone into the Mississippi. "You gonna answer that or just stare at it till it apologizes?" I jump. There's a girl on the other end of the bench. I didn't even hear her sit down. She's maybe seventeen, Black, with a shaved head bleached platinum and a septum ring, wearing a men's Hawaiian shirt about four sizes too big. She's eating sunflower seeds and spitting the shells into a Styrofoam cup with alarming precision. "I wasn't staring," I say. "You were staring." Spit. *Tink.* "First day?" My whole body goes stiff. Every after-school special I ever mocked starts playing in my head: *Stranger danger. Human trafficking. Don't talk to people who know things about you.* "Why?" She shrugs. "Your shoes are too clean. And you keep fixing that strap like it owes you money." I look down. The strap is halfway down my arm. Of course it is. "I'm Reese," she says. "Taylor." She doesn't ask for a last name. I notice that. I also notice she doesn't offer one. "Where you from, Taylor?" "Tennessee." "Ooh. Rocky Top." She grins. Her front tooth is chipped. "What'd you do, set a barn on fire?" "I told my parents I'm trans." I don't know why I say it. It just falls out, like my mouth is sick of keeping it in. My heart is pounding. I brace for the face, the flicker, the recalculation. Reese just nods slowly and spits another shell. "Yeah," she says. "That'll do it." And that's it. No flinch. Something in my chest loosens so fast I almost cry, which would be *so* humiliating that I bite the inside of my cheek until I taste copper. --- She walks me around the Quarter for a while. She knows everything: which café lets you use the bathroom without buying anything, which church hands out sandwiches on Tuesdays, which cops will just move you along and which ones will "ask questions." "Don't sleep in the square," she says. "Don't go with anybody who offers you a place to crash the first night. I don't care how nice they are. *Especially* if they're nice." "You're being nice." She stops. For a second something crosses her face, fast and closed, like a door slamming in the wind. "I'm not offering you a place to crash," she says. "Where do *you* stay?" "Around." "How long have you been here?" "A while." "Where are you from?" "Taylor." She says my name like a warning. "You get one sad story for free. That was yours. I don't do trades." Okay. Noted. Filed. Terrifying. But I keep noticing things. How she flinches when a white SUV slows down on Decatur. How she has a hospital bracelet, the plastic kind, cut off and tucked into her shirt pocket. I only see it when she bends down to tie her boot. How she checks every reflection in every shop window, like she's looking for someone behind her. What's she running from? Or who? And the question underneath that one, the one that scares me more: *Should I be running from her?* --- By sunset, the Quarter changes. Louder. Brass bands on every corner, drunk bachelorette parties in matching pink sashes, the air buzzing. It's beautiful and electric, and I feel like a moth circling a bug zapper. Reese hands me half a po'boy she somehow acquired. I don't ask how. "There's a youth shelter on Frenchmen," she says, not looking at me. "They don't call your parents unless you want them to. They got a counselor who's, like... your people. She's cool." "You stay there?" "No." Too quick. "I'm just saying. It's there." I think about Caleb's text. *r u ok.* I'm not. I'm also, for the first time in forty-eight hours, not completely alone. I don't know if that's the same as safe. The strap slips. This time Reese reaches over and ties a knot in it, tight and practical, like she's done it a hundred times. "There," she says. "Now quit fidgeting. You look like a mark." It holds. I don't know yet if she will.

The adherence to instructions is excellent - the piece maintains first person mixed tense throughout, incorporates substantial internal monologue, includes meaningful dialogue, and follows Taylor through their first day meeting another runaway with clear secrets. The 1000-word target is met appropriately. Character development is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist whose bravado masks deep uncertainty and pain. The internal contradictions - wanting independence while missing family, craving connection while fearing trust - feel psychologically authentic. Reese is skillfully drawn as an enigmatic figure whose own trauma is suggested through subtle details like the hospital bracelet and flinching at white SUVs, rather than exposition. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building tension. Reese's "You get one sad story for free" establishes boundaries while hinting at her own protective mechanisms. The exchanges avoid both unrealistic teen-speak and overly mature philosophical discussions. The prose demonstrates strong technical control with vivid sensory details that ground the reader in New Orleans without overwhelming the narrative. Descriptions like "breathing through a wet dishrag" and "a hangover wearing sequins" are evocative without being purple. The writing maintains consistent energy and pacing. The emotional complexity is well-handled, particularly Taylor's conflicted feelings about family and the mixture of fear and hope in meeting Reese. The piece avoids easy answers while providing enough forward momentum to engage readers. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the voice feels slightly too polished for a distressed teenager, and a few descriptive phrases that border on trying too hard. The ending, while appropriately ambiguous, could have pushed the tension slightly further. The piece succeeds in creating genuine stakes and emotional investment while avoiding both excessive darkness and unearned optimism. It treats serious subject matter with appropriate gravity while maintaining readability. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The world had ended on a Tuesday, which surprised nobody who had ever lived through a Tuesday. It hadn't ended with a bang, or even a whimper, but with a sort of long, sulky beep, the sound a microwave makes when it wants you to know your soup is ready and it disapproves of your soup. After that the lights went out, the screens went dark, and humanity discovered that it had forgotten how to do almost everything, including soup. Midas lived in what had once been a laundromat. He chose it for its defensibility, its thick front window, and the lingering smell of fabric softener, which reminded him of a time when the worst thing that could happen to you was losing a sock. He shared it with Chewy. Chewy was a koala. More precisely, Chewy was an animatronic stuffed koala of the premium range, manufactured in the Before Time by a company that had believed children wanted their toys to have opinions. He had glass eyes, a battery compartment that nobody had opened in forty years, and a voice box that ran on something nobody could identify. Midas suspected spite. "Right," said Midas, spreading a map across the folding table. The map was of a shopping centre, drawn by Midas from memory. The memory belonged to someone else, whom Midas had met briefly, and who had since been eaten. "Today we go to the Megamart." Chewy's head rotated forty-five degrees with a noise like a small drawer opening. "Now With Fifty Percent More Crunch," said Chewy. "Exactly. Food. There's supposed to be a whole aisle nobody's touched. Tins, Chewy. *Peaches.*" Chewy's eyes flickered, which meant either agreement or a loose wire. Midas had long ago decided that, for the purposes of morale, it meant agreement. The flaw in the plan, which Midas had considered for almost four seconds, was that anything untouched in the apocalypse was untouched for a *reason*. Nobody leaves free peaches lying around unless the peaches are guarded, cursed, or on the far side of something with teeth. Midas had a gift. Some people could find water with a stick. Midas could find trouble with nothing at all, in the dark, while asleep. His mother had named him Midas in the hope that everything he touched would turn to gold. Everything he touched turned instead to a situation. --- They set off at dawn. Midas carried a crowbar, a sack, and Chewy, strapped to his backpack so that the koala faced backwards and could, in theory, keep watch. In practice Chewy kept watch the way a weathervane keeps watch: attentively, and to no purpose. The road to the Megamart passed through the Car Park of Sorrows, so called because it was a car park, and also full of sorrows. Rusted hatchbacks stood in neat rows, still waiting for owners who had gone in for milk forty years ago and never come out. "Stay alert," Midas whispered. "Terms And Conditions Apply," Chewy whispered back, at full volume. Something moved between the cars. It was a goat. Midas relaxed. Then he saw the second goat, and the third, and the man behind them wearing a crown made of shopping trolley handles, and he stopped relaxing and started calculating, which in Midas's case meant looking for somewhere to fall over. "Who," boomed the man, "disturbs the Car Park of the Goat King?" "Nobody," said Midas. "Just passing. Big fan of goats." The Goat King narrowed his eyes. They settled on Chewy. They widened. "The Oracle," he breathed. "The what?" "The Speaking Bear of Prophecy! It is written!" The King produced a scrap of cardboard. It had once been part of a box, and bore the words *AS SEEN ON TV* in faded red. "He's a koala," said Midas. "And they're not bears. People always get that wrong—" "Speak, Oracle!" cried the King. "Shall my goats prosper?" There was a long pause. Chewy's head turned with ominous slowness. "Batteries Not Included," said Chewy. The Goat King went pale. The goats, who had been following events more closely than anyone gave them credit for, went feral. --- What followed would later be described by Midas, in the retelling, as a *tactical withdrawal*, and by any honest observer as a man running through the Megamart doors with three goats attached to various parts of his trousers. The untouched aisle was real. It was also untouched because the roof above it had collapsed in the Before Time, creating a skylight, a pond, and an ecosystem. The peaches were there. So was a heron the size of a small wardrobe that regarded the tins as its personal property, and Midas as an interesting new snack. Midas grabbed four tins. The heron grabbed Chewy. "No!" Midas lunged. The shelf he lunged onto had been waiting four decades for exactly this moment, and gave way with something like relief. "Every Little Helps," Chewy observed, from forty feet up, as the heron flapped out through the hole in the roof. --- And so they came home. Midas came home by the road, limping, trouserless below the left knee, with one goat still following him out of what appeared to be genuine affection. He carried two tins of peaches. The other two had been confiscated by the Goat King as tribute to the Oracle, whom the King had watched ascend into the heavens and now worshipped with tremendous enthusiasm. Chewy came home by air. The heron, having discovered that koalas contain nothing but foam and bad advice, dropped him through the laundromat's skylight shortly after sunset, where he landed in a dryer drum with a hollow *bong*. And their reputation came home by rumour. By morning, every wanderer within ten miles knew that the laundromat was the dwelling of the man who walked with goats and the Bear That Flew. Midas opened a tin with the crowbar. It was not peaches. The label had peeled. It was, at a guess, cat food, or possibly soup. He looked at it for a long time. The goat ate the label. Chewy's head turned in the dryer. "You Deserve A Break Today," said Chewy. "Yes," said Midas. "I rather think I do." Tomorrow, he decided, they would try the pharmacy. What, after all, could possibly go wrong? The universe, which had been listening, cracked its knuckles.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and philosophical undertones effectively. The opening line about the world ending on a Tuesday immediately establishes the Pratchettesque voice with its matter-of-fact absurdity and implicit commentary on mundane life. The characterization is well-executed within the constraints of the format. Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose gift for finding trouble feels authentic rather than contrived. The animatronic koala Chewy is cleverly realized - his corporate catchphrases serving as both humor and commentary on pre-apocalypse consumer culture. The dynamic between them works well, with Chewy's random utterances creating genuine comedic moments that also advance the plot. The narrative structure adheres closely to the prompt requirements, moving from planning to execution to inevitable disaster and return home. The mission's failure feels organic rather than forced, arising naturally from the characters' limitations and the world's dangers. The Goat King subplot provides effective escalation while maintaining the story's absurdist tone. The prose demonstrates considerable skill in balancing humor with genuine stakes. Lines like "Everything he touched turned instead to a situation" showcase the author's ability to create memorable, character-defining phrases. The world-building is economical but vivid, establishing the post-apocalyptic setting through telling details like the laundromat's fabric softener smell and the Car Park of Sorrows. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. The heron encounter, while amusing, feels somewhat rushed compared to the more fully realized Goat King sequence. The ending, while appropriately cyclical, could have provided slightly more emotional resonance or character development. The dialogue, particularly Chewy's corporate slogans, serves multiple functions effectively - providing humor, world-building, and plot advancement. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Eleven: The Shop on Heol y Bont The bell above the door didn't ring so much as scream, and a man came through it sideways, rain-soaked, as though the door had been a bullet he was dodging. Mererid Pugh looked up from the till, pencil in her teeth. "We're closing," she said around it. "You're not." He pressed his back against the shelf of Local Interest, breathing hard, and peered through the gap between two Ordnance Survey maps in the window. "The sign says half five. It's ten past four. I can read, you know. Contrary to what the *Mail* says." Through the rain-streaked glass, three men with long lenses jogged past, heads swivelling like gulls. "Ah," said Mererid. "Ah," he agreed. Then he turned, and she understood the gulls. Everyone knew that face. It had been forty feet tall on the side of a bus in Cardiff last spring, brooding over a caption about vengeance. Jasper Vane. Cheekbones you could slice bara brith with. He smiled at her. It was a very good smile. It had clearly been tested on audiences. "Hello," he said, warmly, intimately, as though they'd shared a train compartment and a secret. "I'm so sorry to burst in. I'm—" "Dripping on the Dylan Thomas." He looked down. "So I am. Sorry, Dylan." He stepped off the rug, still smiling. "I'm Jasper." "I know who you are." "Do you?" The smile widened, relieved. "Fan of the show?" "No." The smile stayed exactly where it was, but something behind it flickered, like a lamp on a bad circuit. *Oh, don't,* Mererid told her own face, which was attempting to go warm. *He's a man who does this for a living. You are a woman in a cardigan with a hole in the elbow.* "The films, then," he tried. "Haven't seen them." "Not even *The Pale Crown*? I rode a horse into the sea. Twice. Well, a stuntman did it once, but the second time was me, and I nearly drowned, and the horse bit me." He held up a hand as evidence. "It's a very good film. The critics said I was *luminous*." "The critics," Mererid said, "also liked the one with the talking lorry." He laughed, a real one this time, short and startled, not the practised chuckle from the chat shows. It surprised her how different it sounded. It surprised him, too, from the look of it. "Right," he said. "Right. Tough room." He drifted along the shelves, touching spines. "Lovely shop, though. Smells like a vicarage. You must get loads of people in here asking for your recommendations. I bet you've got wonderful taste. I can always tell." "You can't, though." "I can, actually. I'm very perceptive. It's the job." He leaned an elbow on the counter, settling into it. "For instance, I'd say you're a woman who pretends not to be charmed by anything, but secretly—" "Nine letters," Mererid said. "Sorry?" She tapped the newspaper in front of her with the pencil. "Nine letters. *Actor's vain sort, surprisingly, finds his position*. Second letter's A." He blinked. His hand, halfway to some gesture he'd probably made a hundred times on camera, came down to the counter. "Is that a cryptic?" "No, it's a recipe for cawl. Yes, it's a cryptic." "Hang on." He turned the paper toward himself. His lips moved. She watched the charm drain out of his face and be replaced by something fiercer, narrower, entirely unguarded. He looked about twelve. "*Surprisingly*," he muttered. "That's your anagram indicator. *Actor's vain*, that's—no, that's too many letters. *Vain sort*—" He snatched her pencil. She let him. "V-A-I-N-S-O-R-T. Nine. *Position*. Stationed? No, no. Vain sort, surprisingly... *VARIATIONS*? No, ten—" "You're overthinking it." "I'm *never* overthinking it, I'm under-rehearsed." He scribbled in the margin, crossed out, scribbled. Then he stopped. "Oh, you *pig*. *STATION*—no. It's not actor at all, 'actor's' is the definition-adjacent—no, it's—" He wrote it. "*SAN*—no—" "Take your time," she said, and heard, horribly, that her voice had gone soft. He glanced up. For a second he held her eyes without any smile whatsoever, and Mererid felt it in the backs of her knees, which was absurd, because knees were not for feeling things. "You're enjoying this," he said. "Immensely." "Nobody watches me fail at things. I've got people for that. They stop me before I get there." He looked back down. "*VARIATION* was wrong. It's *AVIATORS*—no, eight. God. Give me a minute." "You do crosswords." "Since I was nine. My nan in Margate did the *Telegraph* every morning with a biro. Never pencil, she said pencil was for cowards." He eyed Mererid's pencil pointedly. "I do them in trailers. Between takes. The crew think I'm learning lines. I let them." "Why?" He shrugged, not looking at her. "Better to be thought diligent than a nerd. Leading men aren't nerds." "Leading men don't hide in bookshops in Aberhenllan, either." "And yet." He grinned. Then he froze, and rapped the page. "*SARTORIAL*—no, doesn't—*RAVISHING*—no, that's just what I'd like you to call me." "I'm not going to call you that." "No," he said, almost fondly. "I'm getting that." Outside, a long lens drifted back past the window. Jasper didn't even look up. Mererid noticed that he didn't. "Here's the thing," he said, pencil scratching. "I'm not used to this." "To crosswords?" "To you. People usually like me by now. It takes about ninety seconds. I've timed it." He said it lightly, but his ears had gone pink. "You're at, what, six minutes?" "Seven." "Seven. And nothing." "Nothing," Mererid lied, and rearranged a stack of bookmarks that did not need rearranging. "It's quite restful, actually." He frowned at the page. "Awful. But restful." She could have told him the answer. She'd filled it in at half three. Instead she came round the counter, stood beside him, close enough to smell rain and something expensive and faintly cedar, and pointed with one finger at the clue. "*Finds*," she said. "Look at *finds*." He looked. She watched him look. Then his whole face opened. "*Finds his position*—it's *vain sort* plus—no—*SITUATION*—no—" He laughed. "I have no idea. I'll get it. Don't you dare tell me." "Wasn't going to." "Can I come back tomorrow?" he asked, and there was nothing practised in it at all. "To finish it. I'm filming up at the castle till Friday." Mererid took her pencil back. Her fingers brushed his and she decided firmly that they hadn't. "We open at nine," she said. "Bring your own pencil." "Biro," he said. "I'm not a coward." The bell screamed as he left. Mererid stood very still in the empty shop for a long moment, then pressed the back of her hand to her cheek and found it burning. "*Duw*," she said to Dylan Thomas. "Don't look at me like that."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Jasper's performative charm gradually giving way to genuine vulnerability, and Mererid's dry, understated Welsh sensibility that masks her growing attraction. The Welsh setting is authentically rendered through place names (Aberhenllan, Heol y Bont), cultural references (bara brith, cawl), and linguistic touches ("Duw"). The bookstore environment feels lived-in and specific, with well-chosen details like the Dylan Thomas books and Ordnance Survey maps. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with each character maintaining a consistent voice. Jasper's desperation to be liked comes through in his escalating attempts at charm, while Mererid's resistance is conveyed through clipped responses and deflection. The crossword puzzle serves as an excellent device - it strips away Jasper's practiced persona and reveals his genuine intellectual curiosity and vulnerability. The romantic tension builds naturally through small moments: the shared focus over the puzzle, the brief eye contact, the finger brush, Mererid's burning cheek. The author shows restraint in not overplaying these moments, allowing the chemistry to simmer rather than boil over. Character development feels earned rather than forced. Jasper's admission about timing his charm offensive and his confession about doing crosswords in secret reveal genuine insecurity beneath the celebrity facade. Mererid's internal struggle between attraction and resistance is well-handled, particularly her self-aware commentary about her cardigan and her decision to let him keep the pencil. The prose style is clean and confident, with some particularly strong descriptive phrases ("cheekbones you could slice bara brith with," "smiled like gulls"). The pacing moves well between banter and quieter character moments. Minor weaknesses include some slightly forced exposition about Jasper's career and a few moments where the charm/resistance dynamic becomes slightly repetitive. The ending, while sweet, borders on being a touch too neat with the setup for future meetings. Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. # The Underhold The door gave without protest. That was the first wrong thing. Aya had expected a ward. She had expected the bite of old scythan glyphwork, or at the very least a lock worth the name. Instead the iron slab swung inward on greased hinges, and the breath of the underhold rolled out to meet them: cold brine, tallow, and beneath it the sweetish rot of rendered blubber, the smell that clung to every dock in Morska like a drowned man's coat. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* Simeon's pocket watch had never seemed so loud. "Well," Katra murmured, her knife already out and pressed flat against her wrist. "Isn't that hospitable." The chamber beyond was a vault of whalebone arches, ribs of some ancient leviathan hauled up from the deep and sunk into the masonry, so that walking into it felt like walking into the belly of the beast. Oil lamps burned along the vertebrae in greasy yellow pools. At the far end, on a plinth of black basalt, sat the artifact. It was a disc of dull green metal no larger than a dinner plate, etched with spirals that seemed to crawl if one looked too long. And beside it, in a high-backed chair of cracked leather, sat Mother Grell. She was not in irons. She was not in the Constabulary's cells on Tallow Street, where half the guild had sworn blind they'd watched her dragged. She sat with one boot crossed over her knee, a brace of pistols across her lap, and she was smiling. "Evening, little moth," she said. "You're late. I'd wagered on midnight." Figures peeled from the shadows between the ribs. There were six, perhaps seven, in oilskin and leather, carrying harpoon-guns and brass-knuckled cudgels. Aya knew some of them. Dunmore. The Hesketh twins. Men she'd drunk with. *Tick. Tick.* "There was no raid," Simeon said quietly. His voice was steady, but Aya heard the dry click in his throat. "Oh, there was a raid." Grell rose, unhurried. "Paid for it myself. Cost me a pretty sum in constables' drink money, and two lads I shan't miss. You want to know who's loyal in a house, Mister Vance, you set the house on fire and see who runs for the silver." Her eyes settled on Aya. "And who runs for the cellar." Aya felt the immateria stir at the edges of her mind like cold water rising in a hold. The shapes that lived there pressed close, eager, whispering in their voiceless way. She could call them. She could open the seam and let the dark come through... The muzzle of a harpoon-gun settled against the base of her skull. "I'd not," said Dunmore behind her, almost apologetic. "I seen what comes out o' you, miss. I'll not be here for it." *Tick.* She let the cold recede. They were disarmed with brisk efficiency. Katra spat and swore in dockside Vessish while the twins bound her wrists; Simeon surrendered his revolver and his silence both. Then Grell crossed the floor to Aya, her boots ringing on the stone, and stopped close enough that Aya could smell the gin and clove-oil on her. "Let's have a look at you, then." Aya did not flinch when the mask came away. She had rehearsed not flinching a thousand times in her mother's mirror. Grell looked for a long moment. Then she laughed, a low, delighted rasp. "Well, bugger me blind. The Ashcombe girl." Someone among the guards drew a breath. Dunmore's harpoon wavered. "Aya Ashcombe," Grell went on, savouring it. "Lord Ashcombe's only daughter. And the witch Ashcombe's too, isn't that right? I was there, you know, the morning they dropped her at Gallows Quay. Fine day for it. The crowd threw fish heads." She tilted her head. "You've got her eyes." *Tick. Tick. Tick.* Aya's mind moved very fast and very coldly, the way it did over her father's anatomical texts at three in the morning. *They'll say it runs in the blood. They'll say he knew. They'll strip him of his seat, and the House will make a show of him, and it will all be because of me.* Her father, who had sat in the dark for a year after the hanging and never once said her mother's name aloud. Her father, who still set two cups at breakfast. *You did this with your eyes open,* she told herself. *Now keep them open.* "Then you know what I'm worth," she said. Grell's smile thinned. "Go on." "Dead, I'm a girl in a gutter. Nobody pays for that. The Constabulary pins it on some dockhand and you've gained nothing but a body you must be rid of." She kept her voice level, drawing-room level, the voice she used on dull suitors. "Alive, I'm the heir to the Ashcombe estate and the proof of a scandal that would topple a Lord of the Admiralty. My father would pay. The Admiralty would pay more to keep it quiet. And there are men in the Brass Assembly who would pay a king's ransom to have the witch's daughter kept close and silent, or to have her delivered to them." "And your friends?" "Are worth nothing to anyone but me." Aya held Grell's gaze. "Which makes them my price. Harm them and I'll give you nothing. I'll open the seam here and now with Dunmore's harpoon in my skull, and you can explain to your lads what crawls out." It was a bluff. Mostly. The silence stretched. Somewhere above them, a steam-whistle keened across the harbour, long and mournful as a whale's song. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* "You hear that, Mister Vance?" Grell said, not looking away from Aya. "Your watch. Loud little thing." She reached into Simeon's waistcoat, drew it out on its chain, and popped the lid. "A quarter past two." She snapped it shut. "The Admiralty's man keeps early hours. I expect we'll have an answer by breakfast." She tossed the watch back to Simeon. It struck his chest and swung there, ticking. "Chain them below," she said. "The girl in the salt cell. Mind her hands. And someone fetch a priest." She glanced at the artifact on its plinth, then back at Aya, and for the first time something like unease flickered across her face. "Just in case." As they hauled her toward the stairs, Aya felt the immateria lap once more at the edges of her mind, patient as the tide. *Not yet,* she told it. *Tick.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through evocative details like whalebone architecture, oil lamps, and the pervasive smell of rendered blubber. The setting feels authentic and immersive. The dialogue is particularly well-crafted, with distinct voices for each character. Mother Grell's speech patterns feel authentically working-class Victorian ("bugger me blind," "I seen what comes out o' you"), while Aya maintains her aristocratic bearing even under duress. The contrast between classes is well-established through speech patterns and behavior. The story adheres closely to the prompt's requirements, hitting all specified story beats: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the supposedly imprisoned guild leader, Aya is unmasked and captured, and she attempts to negotiate using her value as a hostage. The author skillfully avoids writing a fight scene as requested, instead focusing on psychological tension and negotiation. Character motivations feel believable throughout. Aya's quick thinking and aristocratic composure under pressure align with her established background, while her internal struggle about the consequences to her father adds emotional depth. Mother Grell's trap demonstrates cunning leadership, and her knowledge of Aya's mother provides compelling backstory integration. The pacing is well-controlled, with the recurring motif of Simeon's pocket watch ("Tick. Tick. Tick.") creating mounting tension. The author effectively uses this device to punctuate key moments and create rhythm. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the "too easy" entrance immediately telegraphs a trap, and the revelation that the guild leader orchestrated everything follows familiar betrayal patterns. The magical system and political implications are intriguing but could be developed further. The prose occasionally borders on purple, particularly in descriptive passages, but generally maintains restraint. The ending feels appropriately dark and unresolved, fitting the gothic tone without false optimism. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously.
