# Darkroom Revelations The safelight turns everything the color of the inside of an eyelid. I've always liked that about darkrooms. Nobody looks like themselves in here. Your skin goes blood-orange, your hands become strangers' hands, and whatever you'd normally hide under fluorescent light just sort of floats to the surface like an image in the developer tray. Elliot is standing at the tray now, rocking it gently with two fingers, watching a print bloom. His rings, three of them, all tarnished silver he swears came from a dead woman's estate sale, click against the plastic rim. He's wearing that oversized black mohair cardigan again, the one with the unraveling cuff he refuses to fix. "It's coming up too dark," he says quietly. "Pull it at forty-five seconds next time." I say it the way I say everything: like a fact, like a door closing. Then I hear myself and wince. "Or. I mean. It's your call. Maybe you want it dark." He glances at me. In the red light his eyeliner looks almost black, smudged at the outer corners like he did it hours ago and forgot. "Maybe I do." The print surfaces: a self-portrait, double-exposed. His face, and over it a ghostly second face, the same, but with his hair pinned up and his mouth painted. The two images don't quite line up. One eye looks out from each version. I don't say anything. I've learned, over three weeks of these late nights, that Elliot talks into silence the way some people talk into a microphone. If I fill the space, he retreats. So I wait. It is genuinely one of the hardest things I've ever done. My phone buzzes against my hip. I don't touch it. "I've been thinking," he says, transferring the print to the stop bath with the bamboo tongs, "that I don't really know what I am." The vinegar smell of the stop bath rises between us. "Like, as an artist?" I ask, even though I know that isn't what he means. I'm giving him a way out. That's what I tell myself, anyway. Maybe I'm giving myself one. "No." He laughs, small and embarrassed. "Like. Boy. Not boy. Something else. I don't know. I keep taking these pictures and I don't know which face I want to be the real one. Or if either of them is." Here is what I want to do: I want to cross the four feet of sticky linoleum between us and take his face in my hands and tell him exactly who he is, because I've been watching him all semester and I have *opinions*. I want to fix it. I want to be the one who knows. That's my whole thing, isn't it? I'm the one who picks the restaurant, who texts first, who says *come here* and means it. My exes were all sharp-jawed certainties, boys who were so thoroughly boys that I could push against them like a wall. I liked knowing exactly where the edges were. Elliot doesn't have edges. He has soft focus. "You don't have to know," I say finally. "Not tonight." He moves the print into the fixer. His hands are shaking, just slightly. "You're not weirded out?" "Elliot. I have a septum ring and I once dyed my entire wardrobe with beet juice for a performance piece. I'm the last person who gets to be weirded out." That earns me a real laugh, the one where his shoulders come up around his ears. Something in my chest does a stupid little flip. "Can I tell you something?" he says. "Always." "When I'm around you, I feel like—" He stops. Starts again. "You're so *sure*. About everything. And sometimes that makes me want to hide. But sometimes it makes me feel like I could be anything and you'd just... handle it." I don't know what to do with that. I stand very still, the way you do when a bird lands near you. "I don't want to handle you," I say carefully. "I want to—" *What, Dani? What do you want?* "I want to see what you become. I don't want to be the one deciding it." It comes out more honest than I intended. The red light makes everything come out more honest. He sets the tongs down. Rinses his fingers in the wash sink. The water is loud in the small room, and then it stops, and it's very quiet except for the hum of the ventilation fan. "What about you?" he asks. "Does it change anything? For you. If I'm not... a guy, exactly." And there it is. The question I've been circling for three weeks without landing on. I think about the girls I've never let myself look at too long. I think about how I noticed Elliot in September not *despite* the lace collars and the chipped black nail polish but *because* of them. I think about how "attracted to men" has always been a label I wore like a jacket I bought years ago and never checked the fit on. "I don't know," I admit. It's maybe the first time I've said those words to someone I'm interested in. It feels like stepping off a curb I didn't see. "I thought I knew what I liked. Turns out I might just like you." He looks at me for a long moment. Then he picks up the second print, the one of me he took last week without asking, my face turned away mid-laugh, and holds it up to the light. "You look different when you're not in charge," he says. "Better or worse?" "Softer." He sets it down. "I like both." My phone buzzes again. Whoever it is, they can wait. I reach for the next sheet of paper and hand it to him instead of slipping it into the enlarger myself. Our fingers brush. Neither of us pulls away. "Your turn," I say. "Show me what you want to make." In the red dark, uncertain and unhurried, he does.

Her self-awareness about her usual patterns ("My exes were all sharp-jawed certainties") combined with her confusion about this new attraction creates compelling psychological depth. This will form the beginning of a larger story. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). # Stolen Moments in Roma **9:14 a.m. — Piazza di Trevi** The scooter came out of nowhere, a red blur and a shriek of brakes. Ben Ashworth, who had been reading about Nicola Salvi's 1732 design competition, stepped backward into a pigeon, a tourist, and very nearly the fountain itself. The front tyre stopped four inches from his loafers. "*Ma sei scemo?*" The rider flipped up her visor, revealing furious dark eyes and a mouth already moving faster than his phrasebook. "*Cammini guardando il libro come un santo in processione—*" "Sorry, terribly sorry. *Mi scusi.* I'm—*sono*—" He consulted the guidebook, which was absurd, and she watched him do it, and something in her face cracked. "You are checking the book," she said in English, "to know how to apologise?" "It has a section." She laughed. It was a startling, unguarded sound, head thrown back, and Ben felt it land somewhere beneath his sternum. "Alessandra," she said, pulling off a glove. "Ben. Benjamin. Dr. Ashworth, technically, but nobody—Ben." "Technically." She tasted the word like a strange wine. "And what do you do today, Technically?" "The Pantheon at eleven. The Capitoline Museums at two. I have a schedule." She plucked the guidebook from his hands, flipped through his careful pencilled notes, and tossed it into the scooter's top box. "Now you have me." --- **10:02 a.m. — A bar near Campo de' Fiori** "You drink cappuccino after eleven and I leave you on the Tiber," she warned, knocking back an espresso standing at the counter. "It's ten." "Then you have one hour of dignity." He fumbled with coins. When he turned back, the little silver sugar spoon from her saucer was gone, and so was the one from his. She was chatting with the barista, radiant and innocent, her jacket pocket sitting a fraction heavier. He opened his mouth. Closed it. "Something wrong, Ben?" "No," he heard himself say. "Nothing at all." --- **11:30 a.m. — Via Appia, somewhere** He had not been on the back of a motorcycle since a regrettable incident at Cambridge in 1998. Now he clung to Alessandra's waist as she threaded between a bus and a delivery van with inches to spare, the ancient stones blurring beneath them. "You are holding too tight!" she shouted. "I'm holding exactly as tight as I'd like to remain alive!" She laughed and twisted the throttle harder. He shut his eyes, and then, because he realised he was missing everything, opened them. Umbrella pines. Crumbling tombs. The smell of her hair, dust and something like oranges. He had come to Rome to finish a monograph on Augustan funerary inscriptions. He could not remember a single word of it. --- **1:15 p.m. — Mercato Testaccio** She moved through the stalls like weather. She kissed a fishmonger on both cheeks, argued with a cheese seller about his mother, and emerged with lunch: supplì, a wedge of pecorino, two perfect apricots. "Did you pay for those?" Ben asked quietly as they walked away. She bit into an apricot, juice at the corner of her mouth. "Why? Do you want to go back and confess?" "I'm asking as a matter of academic interest." "Academic interest." She held the second apricot out to him. "Take it, Technically. Taste something you shouldn't." He should have refused. He took it. It was the sweetest thing he had ever eaten, and he suspected that was precisely the point. --- **3:40 p.m. — The Aventine Keyhole** A queue of tourists waited to peer through the famous keyhole in the green door, the dome of St. Peter's framed perfectly beyond hedges. Alessandra ignored the queue entirely, towing him to a low wall around the side. "Up." "That's private property." "Everything is someone's property." She was already over. He stood there, forty-three years old, a fellow of his college, a man who ironed his handkerchiefs. He climbed the wall. The garden on the other side was empty and golden, and for a moment they stood alone amid the orange trees, breathing hard, listening for footsteps. She was very close. She reached up and plucked a leaf from his collar, and her fingers lingered at his throat. "Your heart is fast," she observed. "I've just committed trespass." "Is that why?" A door banged somewhere. She grabbed his hand and they ran, and he was laughing, actually laughing, as they tumbled back over the wall. --- **6:20 p.m. — Trastevere** The sky split without warning. Rain hammered the cobblestones, sending tourists scattering, and Alessandra pulled him beneath the striped awning of a tiny gelato shop, where they stood pressed together against the window, soaked. Water ran down her face. She didn't wipe it away. "You are ruining your nice shirt," she said. "You ruined it three hours ago. There's apricot on it." Inside, a boy scooped pistachio for them; she paid for these, he noticed, counting coins deliberately into the boy's palm, and something about that felt like a message he couldn't decode. They ate in silence, watching rain drum on the awning. "Why me?" he asked finally. "You nearly ran me over. You could have just driven away." She considered this, licking her spoon. "Because you apologised to a pigeon." "I didn't—" "You did. You said sorry to the pigeon. In Rome, nobody apologises for anything." She looked at him then, and for once her eyes weren't laughing. "I wanted to see what happens to a man like that when he stops." "And what happens?" The rain was softening. She stepped close, rose on her toes, and kissed him, briefly, lightly, tasting of pistachio and rain, before he could fully understand it was happening. "Ask me tomorrow," she said. --- **9:47 p.m. — Piazza di Trevi** She left him where she'd found him, the fountain lit gold and roaring. The scooter's engine idled. "My guidebook," he remembered. She retrieved it from the top box, pressed it into his hands, and was gone into the traffic before he could say goodbye. Later, in his hotel room, he checked his breast pocket for his return train ticket to London, departing tomorrow morning. Gone. He opened the guidebook. Tucked into the section on apologies, in looping black ink, beside a telephone number: *Some things I take because I want them to stay. — A.* Ben sat on the edge of the bed for a very long time, smiling like an idiot. He did not call to cancel his hotel checkout. He simply extended it.

The dialogue sparkles with authenticity, particularly Alessandra's voice switching between Italian and English, and Ben's flustered politeness. The banter feels natural and serves multiple purposes - humor, character revelation, and plot advancement. The Roman setting is expertly utilized, moving beyond tourist clichés to create genuine atmosphere. The author demonstrates knowledge of the city while using locations to mirror the emotional journey - from the crowded Trevi Fountain to the intimate gelato shop during the rainstorm. The prose maintains elegance without becoming overwrought. Descriptions like "She moved through the stalls like weather" and "The scooter came out of nowhere, a red blur and a shriek of brakes" are vivid without being purple. The writing has a cinematic quality that serves the romance genre well. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Alessandra's motivations remain somewhat mysterious (as intended), while Ben's internal conflict between propriety and desire creates genuine tension. The stolen train ticket revelation provides a satisfying payoff that recontextualizes her earlier thefts as romantic rather than merely mischievous. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the pacing feels slightly rushed, particularly in the middle vignettes, and Ben's transformation, while believable, could have used slightly more internal resistance to make it feel completely earned. The ending, while satisfying, borders on being too neat, though it serves the romantic genre expectations well. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter One: Vega, Neat The gravity hiccups again around second shift, and every glass on my bar does its little shimmy: liquid climbing the walls, hanging there for a heartbeat, then sloshing home. The regulars don't even look up anymore. Old Bartholomew just lifts his mug an inch and waits it out, like a man stepping over a puddle. "Generator's getting moody," he grumbles. "Generator's been moody since before I got here," I say, wiping down the rail. "It's part of the charm." "Charm." He snorts. "Nets, you'd call a hull breach *charming* if it came with a nice view." "Depends on the view, Bart." That gets a wheezy laugh out of him, and I count it as a win. Across the room, the Kessler twins are arguing over a hand of cards, and Doc Imani is pretending not to watch the new ore hauler pilot she's been sweet on for three cycles. Normal night. Warm lights, recycled air that smells faintly of fried tubers, and the hum of the station breathing around us. Then the door hisses open, and a stranger stumbles in like the corridor spat her out. She's Ceph, I think, or part Ceph. Her tentacled dreads are knotted and askew, a few of them twitching independently, the way they do when the owner is scared. Her jacket's scorched at one sleeve. She doesn't look around. She just walks straight to the bar and plops onto the stool at the far end, the one nobody likes because it wobbles. "Vega whisky, neat," she says quietly. Then, after a beat: "Better make that a double." I pull the bottle down. Vega's the good stuff, amber with a faint blue glow when the light hits it right. I pour, and the gravity chooses that moment to dip again. The whisky rises in the glass like it's trying to climb out, then settles. She stares at it. "Does it always do that?" "Every forty minutes or so. You get used to it." I slide the glass over. "First time at the Outpost?" "First time anywhere this far out." She drinks half of it in one go and winces. "Stars. That's strong." "That's Vega. It doesn't do subtle." I lean on the counter, keeping my voice easy. "I'm Nettle. Folks call me Nets." "Oona." She hesitates like she's deciding whether that was a mistake. "Just Oona." "Well, Just Oona, you look like you've had a day." "A week." She laughs, but it cracks in the middle. "Maybe a month. I've lost track." One of her dreads curls around the stem of the glass, gripping it the way a kid holds a blanket. I pretend not to notice. "You running from something," I ask, "or running to something?" Her eyes snap up to mine, bright gold with horizontal pupils. "Why would you ask that?" "Because nobody comes to the rim on purpose, sweetheart. We're the end of every route map. The last stop before nothing." "Is that why they call it the Last Outpost?" "That, and the owner has a flair for drama." That almost gets a smile. Almost. She turns the glass slowly. "What about you? Running from or running to?" Fair question. Rude, but fair. "Little of both," I say. "Mostly from." "Does it work? Coming out here?" "Some days." She nods like that's the answer she expected. Then she reaches into her jacket, and every muscle in my back tightens before my brain catches up. Old reflexes. The kind I've spent four years trying to sand down. But it's only a data chip. Small, silver, scuffed. She sets it on the bar between us and doesn't let go of it. "I need to find someone," she says. "I was told they'd be here." "Lot of someones come through here." "This one's specific." Her voice drops. "I'm looking for a woman who used to work for the Halcyon Syndicate. A fixer. They called her Thorn." The gravity dips again. This time I feel it in my stomach, and I'm not sure the generator is entirely to blame. The whisky in her glass climbs the walls. I keep my hands flat on the counter so she won't see them do anything stupid. "Never heard of her," I say. "You're sure?" "Honey, I pour drinks and listen to miners complain about their ex-wives. Syndicate business doesn't make it out this far." "It does now." She pushes the chip an inch toward me. "The Syndicate's looking for her too. They're three days behind me. Maybe less." Down the bar, Bart has gone quiet. He's not looking at us, but he's not *not* looking at us either. "Why are you telling me this?" I ask. "Because you're the bartender. Bartenders know everyone." Oona's dreads are all moving now, a slow anxious ripple. "And because if I don't find Thorn before they do, a lot of people are going to die. Starting with me." "That's a heavy thing to drop on a stranger over a double." "I know." She finishes the whisky. "I'm sorry. I didn't have anyone else to drop it on." I look at the chip. I don't touch it. Somewhere in the back of my skull, a door I nailed shut a long time ago is rattling on its hinges. "What's on it?" I hear myself ask. "Proof. Of what the Syndicate did at Meridian Station." Her gold eyes hold mine. "Thorn was there. She'd know what it means." Meridian. I haven't heard that word said out loud in four years. I've only heard it in the dark, at three in the morning, when the station's hum isn't loud enough. "Another?" I say, and my voice comes out steady. Good. Small mercies. "Please." I pour. My hand doesn't shake. The gravity holds, for once, and the whisky sits perfectly still, which somehow feels worse. "You got a place to sleep tonight?" I ask. "No." "Room above the kitchen's empty. Smells like tubers, but the lock works." She blinks at me. "Why would you help me?" Because three days isn't a lot of time. Because I know exactly what the Syndicate does when it arrives somewhere. Because this is my home, and these idiots playing cards and mooning over pilots are my people, and I just watched trouble walk in and sit on my wobbly stool. "Outpost hospitality," I say. "We take in strays." She pockets the chip, and I let her. I tell myself it's not a decision yet. I tell myself I'm still just Nets. Across the bar, Bart catches my eye, and for the first time since I've known him, he doesn't make a joke.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in establishing a cozy sci-fi atmosphere while introducing meaningful conflict. The author successfully creates the requested bar setting with vivid details like the gravity hiccups, recycled air, and warm lighting that establish both the sci-fi elements and cozy atmosphere effectively. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building tension. The banter between Nets and Bartholomew establishes their relationship and the setting's casual atmosphere, while the conversation with Oona gradually escalates the stakes. The author achieves the requested 60% dialogue ratio while maintaining narrative flow. Character development is particularly strong. Nets emerges as a complex protagonist with a mysterious past, revealed through subtle hints rather than exposition dumps. Her internal conflict between wanting to help and protecting her new life creates compelling tension. Oona is effectively portrayed as desperate but not helpless, with nice physical details like her twitching tentacled dreads conveying her emotional state. The world-building feels lived-in and authentic. Details like the wobbly stool, the Kessler twins playing cards, and Doc Imani's romantic interest create a sense of community. The gravity fluctuations serve as both atmospheric detail and metaphor for the instability Oona brings. The conflict introduction is well-paced, building from Oona's appearance through her request to the revelation about Meridian Station. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Two: Big Easy, My Ass The first thing I learn about New Orleans is that it smells like somebody spilled a beer on a flower and then set the flower on fire. The second thing I learn is that Darryl, trucker, self-described "man of God," and the owner of the cab I've been riding in for six hours, does not actually believe in kindness to strangers once the stranger asks to stop at a gas station bathroom one too many times. "This is as far as I go, kid," he said, and then the door was slamming and his rig was grinding off down some street called Tchoupitoulas, which I'm pretty sure is just a bunch of letters somebody lost a bet over. So here I am. 7:14 a.m. Backpack. Forty-three dollars. A granola bar that's been crushed into granola dust. And a phone at 12%. Twelve. I stare at that number like it's going to apologize. It doesn't. I switch on battery saver, dim the screen until I can barely see it, and there they are: fourteen missed calls from Mom. Three from Dad, which is weird, because Dad doesn't call anyone. He communicates exclusively through sighs and the Weather Channel. One text from Mom: *Taylor please just tell me where you are.* Not *I love you.* Not *I'm sorry.* Not even my name spelled the way I asked. Okay, that last part's not fair. Taylor works for everything. That's kind of the only thing I ever got lucky with. I put the phone away before I do something stupid, like reply. Or cry on a sidewalk that is actively sticky. --- The French Quarter at eight in the morning is like walking into a party after everybody's gone home but nobody's cleaned up. Guys in rubber boots are hosing puke off the sidewalks. There's a woman in a sequined dress asleep on a bench, one shoe on, looking honestly peaceful. The balconies have ferns dripping over the iron rails, and the buildings are painted colors that would get you a strongly worded letter from the HOA back home. Mint green. Salmon. A purple so loud it's practically yelling. And here's the thing I'm not ready for: it's beautiful. I'm scared out of my mind, I haven't slept, my feet hurt, I'm pretty sure I smell like Darryl's air freshener (Black Ice, which is not a scent, it's a threat), and some dumb part of my chest goes *oh.* Like I've been holding my breath for sixteen years and nobody told me I was allowed to stop. Then a guy in a Saints jersey leans off a doorstep and says, "You lost, baby?" in a voice like a hand on the back of your neck, and the *oh* shrivels up and dies. I keep walking. Fast. Don't look back. Don't look scared. Look like you have somewhere to be. I don't have anywhere to be. That's the whole problem. --- By noon I've learned three more things: 1. Coffee here costs five dollars, which is highway robbery, and I paid it anyway. 2. Beignets are basically fried clouds, and I would die for them, and I have $31.50 left. 3. Every outlet in every café has a little sign that says CUSTOMERS ONLY, and apparently one coffee buys you nineteen minutes of customer status before a lady with a nose ring starts giving you The Look. I'm sitting on the edge of the levee by the river, which is huge and brown and moving like it's got somewhere better to be, when somebody drops down next to me without asking. "You're gonna get robbed sitting like that." I jerk so hard I almost fall in the Mississippi. It's a girl, maybe my age, maybe a little older. Hard to tell. Bleached hair with an inch of dark roots, a denim jacket covered in safety pins, a split lip that's mostly healed. She's eating sunflower seeds and spitting the shells into the river with deadly accuracy. "Sitting like what?" I say, and I clutch my backpack tighter, which is apparently exactly what she means, because she snorts. "Like you've got your whole life in that bag. Which you do. Which everybody out here can tell." She spits a shell. "First day?" I think about lying. I'm good at lying, historically. Ask the smug school counselor. But I'm so tired, and she's the first person all day who's looked at me like I'm a person and not a problem or a target. "Is it that obvious?" "You got bus-station face." She sticks out a hand. "Jules." "Taylor." She doesn't do the thing. The little pause where people look you up and down and try to file you in a drawer. She just nods like Taylor's a perfectly fine name for a perfectly fine human being, and I hate how much that nearly wrecks me. "Where from, Taylor?" "Tennessee." "Ouch." She says it like condolences. "Running from something or running to something?" "Does it matter?" "Kinda. The ones running *to* something usually go home in a week." She looks at the river instead of me. "The ones running *from* something don't." I don't answer. She doesn't make me. --- We walk. Jules knows everything: which church does free lunch on Tuesdays, which cops will let you sleep in Washington Square and which ones will "give you a ride," with air quotes that make my stomach drop. She knows the guy with the Saints jersey, apparently. "Marcus," she says. "Don't. Just, don't. He'll tell you he's got a place for you to crash. You don't want his place." "Noted," I say, and my voice comes out smaller than I want. "How's your phone?" I check. 7%. "Dying." "There's a library on Loyola. They'll let you charge if you look like you're reading." She pauses. "Who keeps calling?" I hadn't noticed her noticing. "My mom." "She the reason?" And I don't know how to answer that, because the answer is yes and no and it's complicated and she cried, she actually cried, and I couldn't tell if she was crying for me or for the kid she thought she had, and I think maybe *that's* what I couldn't stand. "Kind of," I say. Jules nods slowly. She doesn't push. But when I ask her where she's from, she goes quiet in a way that feels like a door clicking shut. "Around," she says. And when I ask where she sleeps, she says, "Depends," and her hand goes to the pocket of her jacket, where there's something heavy, something she keeps touching like she's making sure it's still there. I don't ask again. But I notice. --- By nightfall the Quarter has woken back up. Brass bands on the corners, people with drinks the size of fire hydrants, lights everywhere. Jules says she knows a spot, somewhere safe-ish, and asks if I want to come. *Safe-ish.* My brain is screaming the entire list of ways this could go wrong. I just met her. She won't tell me anything real. She's got something in her pocket she won't show me. Mom would say I'm being naive. Mom would say a lot of things. But Mom isn't here. And Jules is the only person in this whole loud, gorgeous, terrifying city who called me by my name like it was true. My phone buzzes. 3%. Another text. *Please.* I stare at it until the screen goes black on its own. "You coming or what?" Jules says. I shoulder my bag. My whole life in it. "Yeah," I say. "I'm coming."

The 1000-word target is met appropriately. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor's voice feels authentic - the mix of bravado and fear, the sharp observations about their surroundings, and the way they process their family's rejection all ring true. The internal conflict between wanting connection and fearing vulnerability is well-rendered. Jules is efficiently sketched as a character with her own mysteries and street wisdom, avoiding the trap of making her either too helpful or too threatening. The prose quality is high, with memorable imagery ("smells like somebody spilled a beer on a flower and then set the flower on fire") and effective use of concrete details to establish setting. The author captures New Orleans' atmosphere without falling into cliché, focusing on sensory details that serve the character's emotional state. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building tension. Jules's speech patterns feel distinct from Taylor's internal voice, and their conversation flows organically while revealing information about both characters and their situation. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Taylor's conflicted feelings about their family, their simultaneous fear and wonder at New Orleans, and their cautious hope regarding Jules all feel earned rather than manipulative. The piece avoids easy answers while maintaining forward momentum. The pacing is strong, moving from immediate survival concerns through exploration and character introduction to the chapter's end decision point. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world, as it turned out, had not come with a bang or a whimper but with a sort of apologetic *click*, like a kettle switching itself off, and then nothing had ever switched on again. Midas had been nine at the time. He was now thirty-four, and he still resented the name. His mother had chosen it in the belief that everything he touched would turn to gold. Everything he touched turned, with remarkable consistency, into an Incident. "The way I see it," he said, sitting in the doorway of what had once been a branch of Budget Carpets and was now Home, "we have two options." "We have one option," said Chewy, "and you are about to ignore it." Chewy was a koala. More precisely, Chewy was a Cuddle-Pal Deluxe Interactive Companion, Model 7, with Emotional Responsiveness and Seventeen Soothing Phrases. He had outlived his manufacturer, his warranty and, by a considerable margin, the concept of retail. Somewhere along the way he had also outlived his Seventeen Soothing Phrases and developed opinions. Nobody knew how. Midas suspected it had something to do with the lightning storm of the third winter, and Chewy suspected it had something to do with spending twenty-five years in close proximity to Midas. His fur was the grey of old dishwater, one ear was held on with fishing line, and his eyes were two small glass domes that flickered colour whenever he felt strongly about something. This was, the manufacturers had claimed, *delightful*. In practice, it meant Chewy had never once won a game of cards. "Option one," said Midas, "we stay here and eat the last tin." "The last tin has no label." "It's an adventure." "It is *botulism* in a festive wrapper." Chewy's eyes flickered a thoughtful amber. "Option two?" "The Old Depot. Out past the flyover. Wiggins says there's a whole storeroom nobody's opened. Batteries, Chewy. Proper ones." Chewy's eyes went, very briefly, a longing pink. He blinked hard, as though he could force them back to neutral, but it was too late, and they both knew it. Chewy's internal cell had been running on hope and a salvaged torch battery since spring. He tired easily now. Sometimes, mid-sentence, he simply stopped, like a clock that had lost interest in time. "Wiggins," said Chewy, "once sold you a map to the sea." "And we found the sea." "We found a *puddle*, Midas. With a gull in it." "It was a very determined gull." --- They set off after breakfast, which was a biscuit each (Chewy did not eat, but insisted on holding his, for dignity). Midas carried the rucksack, the crowbar, and Chewy, who rode in the front pocket of a baby sling Midas had found in a car in the second year and had never quite managed to explain to anyone. The Old Depot was an hour's walk through the Suburbs, a region where the houses stood in neat rows like teeth in a skull, grinning. The flyover was the tricky bit. It had partially collapsed in the fifth year, and was now home to a colony of goats who had discovered that, without traffic, a motorway was essentially a mountain with better signage. "Don't make eye contact," said Chewy. "With the goats?" "With anything. You have a face that invites consequences." Midas made eye contact with a goat. It was not a long chase, in the sense that it was only about a mile. It was, however, a very *thorough* chase. The goat had clearly been waiting years for someone to stare at it, and it had a lot of feelings to work through. By the time Midas vaulted a crash barrier and fell six feet into a bramble patch, Chewy's eyes were strobing red and white like an ambulance with ambitions. "That," said Chewy from somewhere near Midas's armpit, "was your fault." "The goat started it." "The goat was *eating a traffic cone.* The goat had no plans for the day." --- The Old Depot, when they reached it, was exactly where Wiggins had said it would be, which should have been the first warning. Wiggins was not a man who was often right, and when he was, it was usually by accident and always at someone else's expense. The storeroom door was rusted shut. Midas applied the crowbar, and then his shoulder, and then a vocabulary he had learned from his grandmother. The door gave way with a groan that suggested it had also had a long day. Inside, it was dark, and it smelled of wet cardboard and old promises. Midas lit a candle stub. Shelves. Rows of them. Boxes stacked to the ceiling, each one stamped with a lovely, beautiful word: **BATTERIES**. Chewy's eyes went gold. Not amber, not yellow, but a pure, childlike gold that Midas had not seen since Chewy was new and the world was full of plug sockets. It lit the room better than the candle did. Midas tore open the first box. Empty. The second box. Empty. The third contained a note, written in marker pen, which read: *TOOK THEM ALL. SORRY. — W.* "He *sold* me the map," said Midas faintly, "to a place he'd already robbed." "He's very consistent," said Chewy. His eyes had faded to a dim, grey-blue, the colour of a Sunday afternoon in November. "You have to give him that." It was at this point that the goat arrived. --- They got home at dusk, which is to say they returned in several senses at once. They returned to Budget Carpets, for one. Midas had a limp, a torn sleeve, a bramble in a place brambles should not go, and a hoofprint on his left buttock that would, over the following week, blossom into a bruise the shape of Belgium. They returned to the last tin, for another, which sat on the shelf like a patient creditor. And they returned, inevitably, to the argument. "Tomorrow," said Midas, lying face-down on a remnant of shag pile, "we find Wiggins." "Tomorrow," said Chewy, "we open the tin." "And if it's botulism?" "Then at least it's *our* botulism." There was a pause. Chewy's eyes had dimmed further on the walk home, and now they glowed only faintly, like embers deciding whether to bother. Midas reached over without looking and pressed his thumb gently into Chewy's paw, the way you might hold a hand, or check a pulse. Chewy's eyes flickered a soft, embarrassed pink. "Don't," said Chewy. "Didn't say anything." "Your *thumb* said something." Outside, somewhere in the dark, a goat bleated, triumphant. The world, having ended, carried on regardless, as worlds do. In the morning, they opened the tin. It was peaches. Neither of them ever quite forgave the universe for that.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical observations about human nature, and ability to find profound meaning in mundane post-apocalyptic survival. The author successfully creates a compelling dynamic between Midas, whose name ironically reflects his talent for creating disasters rather than gold, and Chewy, an animatronic koala whose developing consciousness and sardonic commentary drives much of the humor. The story structure follows the prompt precisely: deliberation about the day's mission, the inevitable complications, and return home worse for wear. The mission to find batteries becomes a perfect vehicle for exploring both characters' relationship and the absurdities of their world. The writing maintains Pratchett's signature balance of humor and pathos, particularly in moments like Chewy's dimming eyes and the tender thumb-to-paw contact. The prose demonstrates considerable skill in mimicking Pratchett's voice, from the opening observation about the world ending with an "apologetic click" to philosophical asides about goats and traffic cones. The dialogue crackles with wit and reveals character efficiently - Chewy's pragmatic pessimism contrasting with Midas's determined optimism creates natural tension and humor. The world-building feels authentic to the post-apocalyptic setting while maintaining the absurdist elements that make it distinctly Pratchettesque. Details like the goat colony on the motorway and Wiggins's consistent unreliability create a lived-in feeling. The emotional complexity emerges subtly through Chewy's failing battery serving as a metaphor for mortality and the genuine affection between the unlikely companions. The ending strikes an appropriate note - the peaches represent both disappointment and unexpected grace, and the final line about never forgiving the universe captures the story's blend of resignation and stubborn hope. However, some passages occasionally veer toward being slightly overwrought in their attempts to capture Pratchett's style, and a few metaphors feel forced rather than natural. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 89.1
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Seven: The Arcade** The bell above the door didn't so much ring as shriek. Rain came in with him, and a man in a very expensive coat that was now very wet. "Sorry. So sorry. Is there a back way out of here?" Nia Pritchard didn't look up from the invoice she was pricing. "There's a fire exit. It's alarmed. And it's for fires." "Right. Brilliant. Could I just..." He pressed himself flat against the Local History shelf, out of sight of the window. Outside, three men with long lenses jogged past through the Morgan Arcade, their feet slapping the wet tiles. "Could I just stand here for a moment and pretend to be deeply interested in..." he tilted his head at a spine, "...*The Coal Exchange: A Complete History, Volume Two*?" "Volume One's better. More coal." He laughed, a proper, warm, practised laugh that had been filmed from four angles and slowed down for trailers. Then he waited for her to look up. She didn't. "I'm Callum Ashby," he said. "Okay." "You might know me from..." "I know who you are. You're dripping on the Dylan Thomas." He stepped smartly sideways. "God. Sorry. Is he all right?" "He's a paperback. He's been through worse." She finally raised her eyes, brown, unimpressed, rimmed in reading glasses she immediately regretted wearing. "Are they gone?" He peered round the shelf. "One of them's buying a Welsh cake from that stall. Very committed to his craft." He turned back, and the smile came on like stage lights. "I'm so grateful for this. Really. You're a lifesaver. What's your name?" "Nia." "Nia. That's beautiful. That's Welsh, is it?" "No, it's Portuguese." "Is it?" "It's Welsh, Mr Ashby." "Callum, please." He leaned on the counter. She moved the invoice six inches away from his elbow. "You know, I was born in Penarth." "Your Wikipedia says Surrey." "You looked me up?" Her pen stalled. *Damn.* "My niece has a poster of you. On her wardrobe. You're in a vest." "Ah. The vest." He winced good-naturedly. "The studio insisted. I wanted to wear a jumper. I'm very much a jumper man." "Of course you are." "And we moved to Surrey when I was two. I'm Welsh at heart. Honestly. *Bore da.* See?" "It's half three." "*Bore*... no. Hang on." He snapped his fingers. "*Prynhawn da.*" "Well done. Gold star." She said it flatly, and she did not smile, and it cost her something to not smile, because he'd said it like a boy reciting in chapel. He straightened up. Something in his face faltered. Not much, just a flicker, like a bulb on a dimmer switch. "You don't like me very much, do you?" "I don't know you." "People generally like me when they don't know me. That's sort of the whole business model." "Then it's a good thing I'm not in business with you." "You're in business with *everyone*. You own a shop." He gestured around at the crooked shelves, the leaning towers of unshelved crime fiction, the cat asleep in the window display on a bed of Penguin Classics. "Customer's always right, surely?" "You're not a customer. You're a refugee." "I could be a customer." He grabbed the nearest book off the counter. "I'll buy this." She glanced at it. "*Knitting for the Anxious Beginner.*" "...I am anxious. And a beginner." That did it. A laugh escaped her, short, snorted, horribly unglamorous, and she clapped a hand over her mouth. He pointed at her in triumph. "*There.* There it is. I knew it." "That wasn't for you. That was for the knitting." "It was absolutely for me." "Four ninety-nine." He handed over a twenty. She made change slowly, counting the coins twice, because her hands had developed an irritating need to be busy. He watched her do it. She could feel him watching. "Why did you come to Cardiff?" she asked, then wished she hadn't. Too interested. "Filming. Down the bay. Some Arthurian thing. I play Lancelot." "Course you do." "What does *that* mean?" "Handsome. Bit of a disaster. Ruins everyone's lives and gets a sad ending anyway." He was quiet for a second. "That's... actually a very good note. Can I steal that for the director?" "No." "I'll credit you." "You'll say you thought of it in the shower." "I *do* think of things in the shower." He grinned, then seemed to lose his way in the grin halfway through, like he'd forgotten the next line. "Sorry. That was... I don't know why I said that." "Neither do I." The rain drummed on the arcade's glass roof. The cat stretched and rearranged itself on Jane Austen. Neither of them said anything, and the silence was not the comfortable kind, but not the bad kind either. The kind that hums. "Can I tell you something," he said, and his voice had dropped out of its register, the trailer voice gone, something plainer and more Surrey underneath. "I've been doing this for twenty minutes. The smile. The *Nia, that's beautiful.* And it's not working, and I genuinely don't know what to do with my face now." "Just leave it as it is." "Is it all right as it is?" She looked at him. His hair was wet. There was a raindrop caught on his eyelashes and she was aware, suddenly and alarmingly, of wanting to be the sort of woman who'd reach up and brush it off. "It's fine," she said. "It's a face." "Wow." "It's a *good* face. Obviously. You've been told. You don't need me." "No," he agreed, and then, much quieter, "that's sort of the problem." She had absolutely nothing to say to that. She picked up the pricing gun and priced a book that was already priced. Outside, the Welsh-cake photographer wandered back past the window, mouth full, scanning. Callum ducked. Nia, without thinking, stepped round the counter and stood in front of him, blocking the glass. "He's gone," she said after a moment. "You protected me." "I protected my stock. They'd have been in here, knocking things over." "You stood in front of me like a bodyguard." "I stood in front of the *window*. You happened to be behind it." He stood up, which put him rather close. He smelled of rain and something expensive with cedar in it. "I should go." "You should." "Before they come back." "Before they come back." Neither of them moved. "Do you do deliveries?" he asked. "It's a bookshop, not a Chinese." "Because I'm going to be down the bay for six weeks. And I'm told I need to learn to knit." He held up the book. "Anxiously." "There's a library in the city centre." "There isn't a *you* in the library." "That's the worst line I've ever heard." "I know." He looked genuinely stricken. "I *know*. I've got better ones. I've got loads. They're just not... coming out right, today, for some reason." She pushed her glasses up her nose. Her cheeks were warm, which was the heating, which was broken, which meant it wasn't the heating. "We're open ten till five," she said. "Closed Sundays." He smiled then. Not the lights-on smile. A smaller, crooked, slightly bewildered one that she suspected nobody had ever put on a poster. "*Diolch,* Nia." "Your accent's terrible." "I'll practise." The bell shrieked again as he went. She watched him through the window until he'd turned the corner towards St Mary Street, collar up, knitting book tucked inside his coat like something precious. Then she sat down very carefully on her stool, and said to the cat, "Don't," and the cat, to its credit, didn't.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining consistent quality throughout. The author successfully creates a meet-cute scenario that feels both familiar and fresh, set convincingly in Cardiff's Morgan Arcade with authentic Welsh details that ground the story without feeling forced. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Callum emerges as genuinely three-dimensional - his practiced charm feels authentic rather than cartoonish, and his vulnerability when his usual tactics fail creates compelling dramatic tension. The moment where he admits "I genuinely don't know what to do with my face now" is particularly effective, showing rather than telling us about his fragile ego. Nia is equally well-drawn, with her dry wit and defensive mechanisms clearly established through dialogue and action rather than exposition. The dialogue carries the scene expertly, with each character maintaining a distinct voice throughout. Nia's deadpan responses ("Volume One's better. More coal") and Callum's increasingly desperate charm offensive create natural comedy while advancing both plot and character development. The Welsh language elements are handled with appropriate restraint and accuracy. The prose style is clean and confident, with particularly strong observational details ("a laugh escaped her, short, snorted, horribly unglamorous"). The pacing builds tension effectively through the interplay of banter and underlying attraction. The author shows admirable restraint in not over-explaining the characters' internal states, trusting the reader to understand the subtext. The romantic tension develops organically through their verbal sparring, with moments of genuine connection emerging naturally from the conflict. The scene where Nia instinctively protects Callum from the photographer's view is a perfect example of showing attraction through action rather than internal monologue. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable beats in the romantic development and a few moments where the banter feels slightly too polished for natural conversation. However, these are minor quibbles in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully fulfills all the prompt requirements while maintaining literary quality throughout. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Underhold** The door gave without protest. That, more than anything, should have warned her. Aya stepped through into a long vault of sweating stone, its ribbed ceiling braced with arches of yellowed leviathan bone. Gas lamps hissed along the walls, fed on rendered whale oil. The sweet, rotten stink of it clung to the back of her throat. Their flames guttered in some draught she could not feel, and with every stutter the shadows on the flagstones stretched and contracted like the fingers of something breathing. At the far end, upon a plinth of black iron, sat the reliquary: a squat Scythan casket banded in green-tarnished bronze. Even from forty paces, Aya felt it pulling at the immateria. It was a low, patient ache behind her eyes, like a tooth going bad. "Well," Simeon murmured at her shoulder. "That's rather anticlimactic." "Hush," said Katra. Her hand had already gone to the knife in her boot. "Lamps are lit. Who lights lamps in an empty room?" *Who indeed.* A match flared in the dark beyond the plinth. It touched the bowl of a clay pipe, and a face swam up out of the gloom. It was lined, heavy-lidded, and wholly unbothered. "Punctual," said Mother Varga. "I'll grant you that much." Aya's blood went to slush. The guild leader stepped into the lamplight. She wore the same greatcoat she had worn for twenty years, stiff with salt and old tar. Her irons were not on her wrists. They hung from her belt, polished to a shine, and the chain swung like a trophy. Behind her, the shadows detached themselves into men. There were six of them, big as dockside cranes. Each carried a Hessary repeating carbine, and every brass breech was primed and hissing with pressurised steam. "But the raid," Simeon began. "The constabulary. We *saw* them drag you out in chains—" "You saw what I paid a sergeant eleven sovereigns to show you." Varga drew on the pipe, and its glow painted her teeth orange. "I've been fishing, lad. You cast a bit of bloody meat on the water and wait to see what comes circling. And look." Her eyes settled on Aya. "A shark in a pretty mask." Aya's fingers twitched. The immateria was close here. The casket had worn it thin as muslin, and she could feel the things beyond it pressing their faces to the other side, eager. One word from her and they would come. The nearest carbine swung to her heart. Its gauge needle trembled in the red. "I know what you are, girl," Varga said softly. "I've watched you call your little horrors up out of the black. You're quick. But you're not quicker than two hundred pounds of pressure and a lead ball. Hands where Tobias can see them." *Not quicker. No.* Aya spread her hands. Katra swore, low and filthy, and let her knife clatter to the stones. Simeon was already kneeling. Rough hands took them. Hemp bit into Aya's wrists. It was waxed cord, sailor's work, and it only tightened when she tested it. Then Varga herself came forward, smelling of tobacco and bilge. With one thick finger she hooked the edge of Aya's mask. "Let's see who's been playing at thieves in my house." The porcelain came away. Cold air struck Aya's cheeks, and for one sickening moment she felt more naked than if they had stripped her to the skin. Varga stared at her. Then she laughed, a great wet bark that echoed off the bone arches. "Well, *damn* me. I know that face. I seen it on a broadsheet, eight years back. Pinned up outside the Admiralty gallows." She leaned close. "The Lady Serafina Morrow, hanged for congress with the Unseen. You've her eyes, girl. Her very same eyes." *Don't.* Aya's jaw locked. *Don't let her see.* But the memory came anyway. She saw the drop, the creak of new rope, and the crowd cheering as her mother's slippered feet kicked at nothing. She had been twelve years old, standing in the window of her father's carriage, and he had not let her look away. "Aya Morrow," Varga breathed, savouring it. "Daughter of the Morrow shipping fortune. Heiress to half the whaling fleet in Morska harbour. Moonlighting in my guild. Stealing from my *vault.*" Behind her, Katra made a small, stunned sound. "Aya… is that true?" Aya could not look at her. Two years of trust, and every one of them had been a lie. The truth sat in her gut like cold iron. "You lied to us," Simeon said quietly. He sounded more hurt than angry, which was worse. "I lied to *everyone*," Aya snapped. Then, more steadily, she turned to Varga. "Which is precisely why you're not going to kill me." Varga's brows rose. "Oh?" "Think." Aya's voice was the voice of drawing rooms now, clipped and cool, all vowels and breeding. It was the only armour she had left. "Dead, I'm a corpse in the harbour and a very determined inquiry by my father's solicitors. Alive, I'm leverage over the Morrow fleet. Its manifests, its shipping lanes, its customs officers. Do you know what my father would pay to keep his daughter's name out of the *Morska Gazette*?" "I can imagine." "You can't. Not the half of it." Aya lifted her chin. "Because if it comes out that a Morrow girl inherited her mother's gift, they won't just hang me. They'll pull the charter. They'll seize the fleet. My father will be ruined by nightfall. He knows it. He'd empty the vaults to prevent it." *And he'd never forgive me,* she thought. *If the rope didn't take me first, the family would. Quietly. A sanatorium on the coast, and laudanum until I stopped asking questions.* Varga considered her for a long moment. The lamps sputtered, and the shadows lurched across the floor toward Aya's feet. They were too long and too eager. From the reliquary came a sound like a fingernail drawn slowly across the inside of a coffin lid. The bodyguards shifted. One of them muttered a prayer to the Brass Saint. "And them?" Varga jerked her pipe at Katra and Simeon. "Part of the price," Aya said. "They live, or you get nothing." "Bold. From a girl on her knees." "From a girl who knows her worth." Varga smiled slowly, like a gutting knife sliding home. "Oh, you'll know it, my lady," she said. "Before we're done, you'll know your worth to the very last farthing." She turned to her men. "Take 'em below. The dry cells. And somebody fetch paper. I believe we'll be writing to Lord Morrow." As they hauled her upright, Aya glanced back once at the casket. In the stuttering dark she could have sworn that the thing inside had turned to watch her go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through specific details like "sweating stone," "yellowed leviathan bone," and gas lamps fed on whale oil. The sensory descriptions are particularly effective, from the "sweet, rotten stink" of whale oil to the tactile sensation of waxed rope. The dialogue feels authentic to the setting and characters, with Mother Varga's voice being especially well-crafted - her speech patterns convey both authority and working-class origins. Aya's shift from street thief vernacular to aristocratic "drawing room" speech when revealing her true identity is a nice touch that reinforces character development. The story beats are executed competently: the capture, unmasking, revelation of Aya's identity, and her negotiation gambit all flow logically. The author avoids the requested fight scene while maintaining tension through psychological confrontation. Aya's internal conflict about her deception and fear of her mother's fate adds emotional depth. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The revelation that Varga orchestrated the fake arrest feels somewhat convenient, and her immediate recognition of Aya from an eight-year-old broadsheet strains credibility. The magical elements, while atmospheric, could be more integrated into the immediate tension. Some descriptions, while evocative, occasionally tip toward purple prose ("shadows stretched and contracted like the fingers of something breathing"). The characterization is solid but not exceptional. Katra and Simeon remain somewhat underdeveloped, serving primarily as plot devices for Aya's guilt. The emotional complexity centers mainly on Aya's class deception and family trauma, which is handled competently but predictably. The prose flows well overall, with good sentence variety and pacing. The ending maintains appropriate darkness without false optimism, setting up future conflict effectively. Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gunpowder Rendezvous** A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. It turns like it's thinking about quitting, pushing the haze around without ever clearing it, and Spike Spiegel respects that. He's on his third whiskey and his last cigarette, slouched on a stool with the posture of a man who's melted into it. The bounty sheet on the counter says *Marcus Vey, 4 million woolongs*. Smuggler, murderer, chronic bad tipper. Spike's been told Vey drinks here. So Spike drinks here too. The door bangs open. The woman who walks in doesn't so much enter as arrive, like weather. Black crop top, denim shorts cut short enough to be a statement, a dragon tattoo coiling down her right arm. Two pistols ride in shoulder holsters, and she carries them with the ease of someone who has never once in her life thought about leaving them home. She drops onto the stool beside him and slaps a crumpled paper on the bar. *Marcus Vey.* Spike glances at it, then at her. "Small galaxy." "Fuck off," she says pleasantly, and orders rum. Bacardi, neat, bottle left on the counter. "I was here first." "Yeah? And I'm gonna be here last." She lights a cigarette, inhales like it owes her money. "Name's Revy. Remember it so you can tell the doc who shot you." "Spike." He eyes her pack. "You gonna finish all those?" She stares at him for a long second, then flicks one across the counter. He catches it without looking. That earns him the ghost of a smirk. They drink. It becomes a contest without either of them agreeing to it. Glass for glass, the bartender watching like he's refereeing a slow-motion car crash. Revy talks with her hands, mostly in profanity. Spike talks barely at all, which seems to irritate her more than anything he could say. "You're one of those," she says, pointing her glass at him. "Guys who think being quiet makes 'em deep." "And you're one of those who thinks being loud makes you right." "I *am* right. I'm always right. The ones who disagree stop disagreeing real fast." He laughs, a low, easy sound, and she hates how it hits her somewhere under the ribs. She's a good judge of dangerous men, and this one's the worst kind: the kind who doesn't seem to care whether he lives. She's seen that look in the mirror. "Your eye's weird," she says. "So I've been told." "One of 'em doesn't look at me right." "It's fake." He taps his temple. "Bad depth perception. Makes it hard to tell how close things are." Revy leans in, deliberately, until he can smell the rum and gunpowder on her. "How close is this?" "Close enough," Spike says, not moving back an inch. The door opens again. Marcus Vey walks in with four friends, sees two bounty sheets on the bar, and does the math faster than anyone expects. Then the room explodes. Revy's Berettas are out before the first shot lands, both hands, both barrels, the Cutlasses barking in a rhythm like a drumline. Spike rolls off his stool, Jericho already in his hand, and puts a round through a thug's shoulder from under a table. Bottles shatter. The ceiling fan takes a bullet and finally, mercifully, stops. "That one's mine!" Revy shouts, vaulting the bar. "You're shooting at *everyone*!" "Yeah, so they're *all* mine!" A guy with a shotgun comes at Spike from the side. Spike sidesteps, catches the barrel, and folds the man in half with a knee and an elbow, flowing like water, like it's choreography he learned in another life. Revy sees it mid-reload and, for half a second, forgets to shoot. Vey bolts out the back. They both chase him, shoulder to shoulder, shoving each other through the doorway, and they both watch his taillights vanish down the rain-slick street. Silence. Sirens, somewhere far off. "You lost him," Revy says. "*We* lost him." "You were in my way." "You shot the fan." --- The motel is called the Starlite, and half the letters in the sign are dead. They're only here because it faces the garage where Vey's car is registered, and they're only sharing a room because neither of them has the money for two and neither will let the other stake out alone. At least that's what they tell themselves. The room smells like mildew and cheap detergent. One bed. Spike sits on the edge of it; Revy leans against the dresser. Rain taps the window. It takes about four minutes for the guns to come out. It isn't about anything, really. He reaches for his jacket; she draws. She draws; he draws. Now there's a Beretta leveled at his chest and a Jericho pointed at hers, the distance between them exactly one bad decision wide. "You were gonna take the shot," she says. "At the bar. When it was over. Take me out, take the whole bounty." "So were you." "Damn right I was." Her voice is low, rough. "Still might." He stands, slow, and steps closer until the muzzle of her gun is pressed against his shirt. She doesn't pull the trigger. He doesn't lower his. "You know what your problem is?" Spike says quietly. "Enlighten me, cowboy." "You don't trust anybody." "And you *do*?" "No." A crooked smile. "That's why I like you." Her breath catches. His eyes, the real one and the fake one, stay on her mouth a beat too long. She could close the gap. So could he. The rain keeps falling, and the only sound in the room is two people breathing like they've been running. "I'm not a good person," Revy says. "Not a bad one either. I'm just here." "Whatever happens," Spike murmurs, "happens." Neither of them moves. Outside, an engine turns over. Headlights sweep the curtains: Vey's car, pulling out of the garage. They look at each other, the moment hanging, cracked, unfinished. Then Revy grins, sharp as broken glass, and shoves past him to the door. "Last one to him buys the drinks." Spike holsters his gun, lights her stolen cigarette, and follows her into the rain. Some standoffs don't end. They just wait for the next round.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding. The author captures both Spike and Revy's voices authentically - Spike's laconic fatalism ("Whatever happens, happens") and Revy's aggressive profanity-laced dialogue feel true to their source material. The characterizations are nuanced, showing Spike's fluid martial arts background and Revy's dual-wielding gunplay while maintaining their psychological complexity. The prose style is confident and evocative without becoming overwrought. Descriptions like "she carries them with the ease of someone who has never once in her life thought about leaving them home" efficiently convey character through action. The bar scene establishes atmosphere effectively with details like the "lazy ceiling fan" that "turns like it's thinking about quitting." The action sequence is well-choreographed, maintaining clarity while showcasing each character's fighting style. The transition from bar fight to motel standoff follows logically and builds tension appropriately. The sexual tension is handled with restraint - present but not gratuitous, fitting the noir atmosphere. The dialogue crackles with personality and subtext. Exchanges like Revy's "You're one of those guys who think being quiet makes 'em deep" followed by Spike's counter feel natural while revealing character dynamics. The banter during the gunfight adds levity without undermining the danger. The ending avoids forced resolution, staying true to both characters' inability to fully trust or commit. The unresolved tension feels earned rather than artificially maintained. The final lines provide satisfying closure to the immediate scene while acknowledging the ongoing psychological standoff. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable beats in the setup and a few moments where the prose edges toward being overly stylized, though it generally maintains good balance. The piece successfully fulfills all prompt requirements while maintaining narrative integrity.
